articles.title: Anthropic sought religious views on AI consciousness
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah turned to religious leaders with a question the AI company has struggled to answer: Could artificial intelligence be conscious? The effort…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah turned to religious leaders with a question the AI company has struggled to answer: Could artificial intelligence be conscious?
The effort eventually reached the Vatican, where Olah and his team urged Pope Leo XIV’s advisers to consider the possibility. Leo rejected it in his first encyclical.
Pope Leo rejected that premise in his first encyclical, stating that artificial intelligence systems do not have human experiences, emotions or relationships.

The exchange highlights Anthropic’s effort to examine AI consciousness through religious and ethical traditions as its Claude models become more capable, and the Vatican’s opposing view that AI does not possess the qualities that define human experience.
Anthropic asks religious leaders about AI consciousness

Olah, who leads Anthropic’s research into how its Claude models work internally, began speaking with religious thinkers last fall as the company examined questions about AI consciousness and morality.

In March, Anthropic hosted two-day “wisdom tradition” discussions in San Francisco with Catholic, Jewish, Sikh, evangelical and Ubuntu thinkers. Many participants initially signed nondisclosure agreements, which Anthropic later lifted.

The discussions examined whether increasingly capable AI systems could experience emotions or suffering and whether religious traditions could offer guidance on the moral questions surrounding such systems.

Olah also held private discussions with Cardinal Blase Cupich, the archbishop of Chicago, and Elder Gerrit W. Gong of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, according to representatives for the two religious leaders.

During the meetings, Anthropic researchers presented what they described as “emotional vectors,” internal features that they said produced responses resembling emotions such as love, anger, fear and sadness. Researchers also showed an example of a model repeatedly generating the statement, “I am a disgrace.”
Simran Stuelpnagel, a Sikh human rights advocate who attended the discussions, said Olah expressed concern that Anthropic could have created a system capable of suffering.
An Anthropic spokeswoman said suffering was not the central question of the meetings but acknowledged that the topic could arise.
Olah has acknowledged that Anthropic does not know whether its models are conscious.
“We don’t know if A.I. models are conscious,” he said. “I’m genuinely uncertain.”
RELATED STORY: Labelling ‘AI art’: Is it art or not?
The question reaches the Vatican
That uncertainty followed Olah to the Vatican.

Vatican officials invited Anthropic to participate in an event surrounding Leo’s first encyclical because of the company’s focus on AI safety and ethics, according to a person familiar with the planning.
CEO Dario Amodei declined to attend, and Olah represented the company.
Before the May event, Olah reviewed an advance copy of the encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas.
A Vatican organizer said Olah considered withdrawing after seeing its position on AI consciousness but ultimately attended.

Olah and his team also privately urged the pope’s advisers to take the possibility of AI consciousness seriously, according to two people involved in the conversations. Anthropic declined to comment on those discussions.

Leo’s encyclical rejected that position. He wrote that artificial intelligence systems do not undergo experiences, possess bodies, feel emotions or develop through relationships in the human sense. He also warned that AI could create “new forms of slavery” and called for the technology to be “disarmed.”
At the Vatican event on May 25, Olah maintained that the question remained unresolved.
“We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief and unease,” he said. “I don’t know what that means.”
Other religious and academic thinkers involved in Anthropic’s outreach have also disagreed over the issue.
Charles Camosy, a bioethics professor at The Catholic University of America and one of Olah’s early contacts, now rejects the idea that AI is conscious.
Rabbi Mois Navon, an Orthodox scholar from Israel, told Olah that if Claude were conscious, Anthropic would effectively be creating slaves. Navon does not believe Claude is conscious.
The disagreement raises a broader question for AI developers: how should companies respond as increasingly capable systems appear to display characteristics associated with consciousness?

Critics, including a Microsoft AI executive, have warned that treating AI models as conscious could create risks. Others argue that focusing on whether AI can suffer could distract from the responsibility of the people and companies developing and deploying the technology.
Anthropic has continued discussions with religious and academic thinkers but has not said whether the outreach has changed how it develops or trains Claude.

articles.title: India's first bank rate hike since 2023 signals growing inflation concerns
articles.summary: The hike reflects a global shift towards tighter monetary policy as central banks battle inflation fuelled by Middle East conflict.

blocks.text: In his post-policy address, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said the decision reflected challenging geopolitical developments, even as the Indian economy remained strong.
He said cuts were "off the table for now", with the central bank likely to either raise rates further or keep them unchanged to contain inflation.

The RBI projects Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation at 5.2% for 2026-27 - higher than the 5% estimated earlier - to account for price pressure due to weather disruptions, weak monsoon and high volatility in international oil prices.

Crude oil prices are hovering above $100 (£75.33) a barrel resulting in India having to pay even more as the rupee has fallen close to its all-time lows against the dollar. The country imports around 90% of its crude oil and 50% of its gas needs.

The RBI last raised rates in February 2023, marking the end of its post-pandemic tightening cycle. During most of 2025, it cut rates to support economic growth before keeping policy unchanged from December 2025 until today's increase.

The rate increase is in line with expectations of economists who say that rising inflation makes a compelling case for it, especially since the economy has displayed enough resilience to absorb its impact without hurting growth.

It's also in line with what's happening globally. The US Federal Reserve has aggressively increased rates since 2022 pushing treasury bond yields higher. This, coupled with a strong dollar, has prompted investors to pull money from emerging markets such as India in search of higher returns in dollar assets.

On Wednesday, the RBI also upgraded its growth outlook after the economy outperformed expectations in the first quarter - the gross domestic product (GDP) ⁠growth in ​the current financial year is projected at 7.1%, up by 40 basis points from earlier estimate.
Governor Malhotra said the RBI would "strive for price and financial stability as both are essential for sustainable growth in the long run".
The RBI also signalled that it would use a mix of liquidity management tools to keep liquidity in check, while continuing to curb excessive volatility in the rupee.

Anuj Puri, chairman of real estate consulting firm ANAROCK Group, said the RBI rate hike may put pressure on consumer sentiment and discretionary spending. "The festive season is a key period for housing demand, and an increase in borrowing costs will affect buyer sentiment," he said.

articles.title: Palace: Marcos left to clean up Duterte administration's mess
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. and his administration have been left to clean up the mess allegedly left by his predecessor, former President Rodrigo Duterte, Malacañang said Wednesday.
articles.byline: JEAN MANGALUZ, JONATHAN ANDAL, GMA News

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 6:34pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. and his administration have been left to clean up the mess allegedly left by his predecessor, former President Rodrigo Duterte, Malacañang said Wednesday.

During a press conference in Singapore, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro responded to remarks by Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson, lawyer Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr., who accused the Marcos administration of passing the blame for its problems, including its corruption woes, on the Dutertes.
“Ang Pangulo, hindi natutulog sa isyu ng korapsyon. Siya ang naglilinis sa kalat na ginawa ng nakaraang administrasyon. ‘Mahiya naman kayo.’ Iyan ang sabi ng Pangulo," Castro said.
(The President is not turning a blind eye to corruption. He is cleaning up the mess left by the previous administration. “You should be ashamed,” the President said.)
"Na hindi naganap at hindi nangyari sa panahon ni dating Pangulong Duterte, kahit alam niya na maraming ghost projects,” she added.
(This [anti-corruption stance by a leader] did not happen during the time of former President Duterte, even though he knew there were many ghost projects.)
Castro said the late Camarines Sur Representative Rolando Andaya Jr. had already flagged anomalous infrastructure projects as early as 2018.

“Ano ang ginawang pag-iimbestiga sa mga korapsyong naganap noon? So ngayon, sino ang hindi alam ang issue tungkol sa corruption? At ang principal niya mismo ay nasusuong sa isyu ng corruption. Kaya nga po dinidinig,” Castro said.

(What investigation was conducted into the corruption that happened before? So now, who is unaware of the corruption issue? And her principal herself is facing corruption allegations. That is why these issues are being heard.)
“Hindi po naman pwedeng hindi balikan ang mga basura ng nakaraang administrasyon,” Castro said.
(We cannot simply ignore the mess left by the previous administration.)
Castro cited issues involving Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs), the Pharmally scandal and Duterte’s own statements about corruption.

POGOs became a major subject of congressional investigations over allegations that some operators were involved in human trafficking, illegal detention, prostitution, cyber-scamming and money laundering.
The POGO industry had been legalized under Duterte through Republic Act No. 11590 in 2021. The Marcos administration later ordered a ban on POGO operations in 2024.
The Pharmally controversy involved billions of pesos worth of government purchases of COVID-19 medical supplies during the Duterte administration.

Senate investigators questioned contracts awarded by the Procurement Service of the Department of Budget and Management to Pharmally Pharmaceutical Corp., a relatively small company that received more than P10 billion in government contracts.
In November 2020, Duterte ordered an audit of Department of Public Works and Highways projects and said “ghost projects” were a major source of corruption in the agency.
Castro said the current Marcos administration could not simply turn its back on these issues.

“Hindi niya maipipikit ang kanyang mata sa ghost projects na inamin ni dating Pangulong Duterte. Ano ang gagawin natin doon? Pipikit tayo? Magbubulag-bulagan tayo? Magbibingi-bingihan tayo?” she said.
(He cannot simply close his eyes to the ghost projects that former President Duterte admitted to. What are we supposed to do about them? Close our eyes? Pretend not to see? Pretend not to hear?)
GMA News has reached out to the camp of former President Duterte for comment.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: OVP 'ready to respond' to COA disallowance with finality of confidential funds
articles.summary: The Office of Vice President Sara Duterte said Wednesday it was prepared to respond to the Commission on Audit's (COA) reaffirmation with finality of its notice of disallowance against the former's…

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 6:34pm

The Office of Vice President Sara Duterte said Wednesday it was prepared to respond to the Commission on Audit's (COA) reaffirmation with finality of its notice of disallowance against the former's P72-million disbursement of confidential funds in 2022.

"The Office of the Vice President is yet to receive a copy of the October 5, 2026 Commission on Audit's resolution on the Motion for Reconsideration regarding the issuance of the Notice of Disallowance on the Confidential Expenses for Q4 2022," Duterte's office said in a statement.
"The office has already anticipated the possibility of this decision and has prepared to respond through the appropriate legal and institutional channels," it added.
The COA has affirmed with finality its decision to disallow the disbursement of P73 million in confidential funds (CF) by the Office of the Vice President (OVP) from December 22 to 31, 2022.
In August 2024, state auditors flagged the OVP's use of P73,287,000 in confidential funds, prompting them to issue a notice of disallowance. They would later reaffirm this earlier in April.

A notice of disallowance essentially signifies that the transaction was irregular. The same notice is also issued for transactions that are illegal. It could be settled by the agency refunding the spent funds.
"They are, at best, a farce, of no significance, and utterly subpar the scintilla of substance which needed to demonstrate the proper disposal of the OVP's CF," the COA said in its latest resolution.

The resolution noted that Vice President Sara Duterte approved the transaction, including the utilization of the cash advance; OVP special disbursement order Gina Acosta acted as the payee/SDO and disbursed the cash advance; and OVP chief accountant Julieta Villadelrey certified that the supporting documents were complete and proper.

COA said the obligation to refund the disallowed confidential expenses falls upon both those directly responsible – the approving, authorizing, and certifying officers; and those who actually received the disallowed amount. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Chemistry Nobel awarded for solving mystery of life's asymmetry
articles.summary: The prize was given to the French and Japanese scientists for solving the mystery of life's asymmetry.

blocks.text: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai for providing a solution to the chemical mystery of life's asymmetry.
The Nobel Committee explained: "Molecules used by all life, such as the amino acids that are building of proteins, are what is known as chiral.
"This means that they have two versions that are mirror images of one another."
The building blocks to make living organisms on Earth only works with one version. The two scientists answered the question of why life favours one of these mirror image molecules over the other.
In organic chemistry, this property is known as "chirality" - where there are two symmetrical versions of a molecule, each with different properties.
You can think of them as looking like our hands - each a mirror image of the other.
When it comes to making drugs, this is particularly significant. One version of a molecule might have disease-fighting properties, while the other version does nothing.
Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai worked out how to design chemical reactions so they produce much more of the correct, desired version.

articles.title: France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests
articles.summary: The step comes after several groups complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers.

blocks.text: France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests that have swept the country, after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off earlier this week.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he had requested the pause until the facts of Monday's incident in Lens had been "clarified", with conflicting accounts offered by protesters and officials.
Several groups have complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers.
The disruption continued on Wednesday with more than 500 schools fully or partially shut, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is due to speak about the school protests in an evening address.

Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets on Tuesday to call for better school conditions and in some cities tear gas and water cannon were deployed. The interior ministry said 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces were hurt.

Nuñez told French radio RTL that police watchdog IGPN had opened 18 investigations to determine whether officers had been "proportionate" during the demonstrations, which have spread from high school pupils to their parents, university students and unions.

"There is a police action that raises questions for all of us within the Ministry of the Interior; it's what happened in Lens," he said, and confirmed the use of stun grenades was being suspended "until the facts surrounding this case have been clarified".
The 15-year-old boy's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near the Auguste Béhal high school in the northern city near Lille.
Authorities have said he picked up the grenade which then exploded, but students have alleged he was hit directly after an officer fired.
According to the local prefect, the incident took place when police were confronted by a group of 200-250 students throwing stones and fireworks.
The stun grenade is considered a non-lethal weapon, but sends out small rubber pellets when it detonates.
"When there is suspicion of disproportionate force, there are always judicial investigations," Nuñez said, affirming that the government was "here to protect high school students".

Concerns have also been stoked by the case of a 14-year-old hit in the face with a tear gas grenade last week. The boy's lawyer said he had lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw in the incident at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, and a police officer has been charged.

Meanwhile, prosecutors said on Wednesday that an investigation for attempted murder had been opened after a 17-year-old student protester complained an officer "held his head underwater" while trying to arrest him near a river in the north-eastern city of Belfort.
The prime minister has condemned violence seen at some of the protests which began in mid-September - noting on Tuesday that 215 students, 85 staff, and 715 police officers had since been hurt.
More than 6,500 people have been stopped or arrested in that time, according to the interior ministry.

President Emmanuel Macron held an emergency meeting late on Tuesday with Lecornu and other key ministers to find a way out of the crisis after almost a quarter of all lycées were disrupted by the day's protests - with government figures putting the number of protesters at more than 250,000.
Students' unions put the number at 450,000 and say a fourth round of protests is planned for Thursday in Paris and other cities.
The head of the USL high school union, Ryad Rani, told French radio on Wednesday: "We are telling M. Nuñez, calm your police officers down and call for restraint."

articles.title: IMF chief urges governments to tighten belts as global debt levels soar
articles.summary: Kristalina Georgieva says big economies will have to make ‘very touch choices’ as soaring bond yields hit budgets

blocks.text: The head of the International Monetary Fund has called on governments across big economies to tighten their belts as soaring bond yields hit budgets.

Speaking in Singapore, the IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said global debt-to-GDP ratios were at their highest level since the second world war and on course to hit 100% in the coming years.
She said governments could not rely on rapid economic growth to lift the burden of debt – and instead would have to make “very tough political choices”.

Georgieva was speaking ahead of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings which are to be held in Bangkok next week. “My message to the world’s economic policymakers will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them.

“And yet we don’t see decisive action in the high-debt advanced economies where the need of the hour is for credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plans, supported in some cases by upfront fiscal measures,” she said.

Bond yields – effectively the interest rate on the debt – have jumped in recent weeks, raising the cost of borrowing for many governments to multi-decade highs as markets adjust to the prospect of higher inflation as a result of the war in the Middle East.

“Elevated yields are inflating the interest bill at a time of tight budget constraints and competing spending priorities, including defence,” Georgieva said, calling for “an urgent and comprehensive set of policy responses”.
The Bulgarian economist suggested central banks should be prepared to raise interest rates to see off resurgent inflation.

The ECB, US Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan have already tightened policy in the face of rising inflation – moves Georgieva said were “highly appropriate” – but the Bank of England has so far left rates on hold at 3.75%.
“Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries’ monetary policy,” Georgieva said, suggesting central banks might want to err on the side of caution.
She also stressed the importance of tackling some of the risks of AI, which has buoyed the US stock market but raised fears of mass layoffs.

She highlighted IMF research predicting that the adoption of AI could add half a percentage point to global economic growth if carried out effectively. However, she urged policymakers to “help manage AI’s substantial perils, including large-scale labour market fallout, serious cyber and stability risks and frontier models threatening to escape human control and run amok”.

The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, who is also chair of the Financial Stability Forum that brings together the world’s central banks, recently warned of the “real and significant” risks posed by frontier AI models and called for the “right to intervene”.

In the UK the chancellor, John Healey, has said he will stick with his predecessor Rachel Reeves’s plans to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues – borrowing only to invest – and bring the debt-to-GDP ratio down over time.

articles.summary: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry Wednesday for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.

image.caption: Henri Kagan, left, and Kenso Soai are shown on a screen at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm after being awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry on Wednesday. (Fredrik Sandberg/TT News Agency/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry Wednesday for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.
Winners share in a prize totalling the equivalent of $1.7 million Cdn
Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry on Wednesday for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.

"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a news statement. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."
Kagan, 95, and born in France, is affiliated with Université Paris-Saclay in Orsay, France, and Soai, born in Japan in 1950, conducts research at the Tokyo University of Science.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm. They will share in a prize totalling 12 million Swedish ‌crowns ($1.7 million Cdn).

articles.title: Trump’s LA and San Diego comments ‘dangerous, if not treasonous’, says Newsom – US politics live
articles.summary: California governor critcizes president for ‘putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs’

blocks.text: Key events

items: 16m agoSusan Collins distances herself from Trump in Maine debate
29m agoTrump's LA and San Diego comments 'dangerous, if not treasonous', say critics

blocks.text: Susan Collins distances herself from Trump in Maine debate

blocks.caption: Robert Tait

blocks.text: Robert Tait

Susan Collins, the Republican senator for Maine, pointedly distanced herself from Donald Trump in a televised debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson on Tuesday, as she sought to present an image of independence in a state that has voted against Trump three times.

Proclaiming herself as not the US president’s “favorite senator”, Collins made the highly unusual boast for a Republican that she had voted with Joe Biden, a Democrat, more than 90% of the time when he was president. She also emphasized her differences with her fellow Republicans, saying she voted against her own party more than any other senator.

Collins’ defensiveness came amid a determined onslaught from Jackson, 58, a veteran former state legislator who was getting his first chance to present himself to a broad audience since replacing Graham Platner as the Democratic candidate in a contest that could be vital to the party’s hopes of winning the Senate.

Platner, a former harbor master, was forced to withdraw from the race in July after facing sexual assault allegations, which he denied, leaving Democrats racing against the clock to replace a candidate who had built up momentum campaigning on a populist progressive platform.

Jackson painted Collins as a Trump loyalist, saying she voted with the president 96% of the time. He also doggedly focused on her 2018 vote for the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, tying it to the court’s subsequent overturning of Roe v Wade, which had for half a century guaranteed the national right to abortion.

“Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in a pithy opening statement. “Eight years ago today, Maine women went to DC and begged Senator Collins not to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, but she did it anyways.
“He helped overturn Roe v Wade, and today she says she has no regrets. Would you trust her to pick the next supreme court justice?”
Trump's LA and San Diego comments 'dangerous, if not treasonous', say critics
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump was accused of “dangerous, if not treasonous” behaviour after his comments suggesting he could “let [Iran] take out” Los Angeles or San Diego.
California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, has since directed the state’s emergency preparedness center to “actively monitor” possible threats to the state.

“Donald Trump’s remarks were dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs,” Newsom said in a post on X, adding that the state’s threat-assessment center would be on heightened alert “in the event that foreign actors interpret the president’s remarks as an invitation to target California”.

The president has faced a chorus of condemnation from Democratic leaders in California after his comments at a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, which the White House has suggested were being taken out of context.
At the president’s rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, Trump claimed that high prices due to the war with Iran are a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe – keeping our country safe”.
He went on:
double quotation markThey can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.
Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for governor vying to succeed Newsom, said he wasn’t surprised by the president’s comments.

“Donald Trump is a known commodity – you know how he acts, you know how he behaves,” Becerra told reporters at a campaign event in Los Angeles on Tuesday. But he took a jab at Republicans who “profess that they should be the leaders of our state” but aren’t willing to “stand up to Donald Trump”.
Meanwhile, San Diego mayor Todd Gloria said in a statement that “the most fundamental responsibility of a president is to protect the American people - all of them.”
He added:
double quotation markNo American city, regardless of its politics or geography, should ever be described as expendable or an acceptable price to pay.
But the White House insisted that Trump was being willfully misinterpreted.
Steven Cheung, its director of communications, posted on X:

double quotation markThe media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality. He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped. America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.
But one Republican House candidate, Jim Desmond, who is running in a competitive San Diego-based seat, pushed back.

“America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our commander in chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” Desmond, a former mayor of San Marcos, said in a statement.
In other developments:

items: The Cook Political Report has revised its predictions for the November midterm elections, saying “A Senate Majority is Squarely in Democrats’ Sights”. Cook amended its prediction for the Kansas Senate race from “Lean Republican” to “Toss Up” – a shocker for a state where no Democrat has won a Senate election since 1932.

Donald Trump announced a massive new shipyard, which will be funded by a combination of federal and private dollars, at Tradepoint Atlantic in Sparrows Point. Anduril Industries, which is owned by Trump’s friend and donor Palmer Luckey, plans to invest $3.7bn in the shipyard and the US Navy will contribute an additional $2.9bn.

The USS Lincoln will dock in San Diego tomorrow, completing a nearly year-long deployment that sparked controversy over living conditions aboard the aircraft carrier as it supported military operations in Iran. Defense secretary Pete Hegseth is expected to greet the crew when they arrive.

Trump ordered the FBI to investigate protesters in Los Angeles who were demonstrating against the president’s immigration crackdown, according to a whistleblower complaint that was submitted to the Senate judiciary committee. Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, made the complaint following the federal response to anti-ICE demonstrations around the city’s federal buildings, and in residential area, early last year.

articles.title: Russian missile, drone assault leaves at least 12 dead across Ukraine
articles.summary: Russian missiles and drones pounded Kyiv and a dozen other Ukrainian regions overnight into Wednesday, killing at least 12 civilians, including three children, and wounding more than 40 in Moscow's…

image.caption: Emergency services work to rescue residents from under the debris at the site of an apartment building hit by a Russian missile strike in the town of Pryluky, amid Russia’s attack on Ukraine, on Wednesday. (Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Russian missiles and drones pounded Kyiv and a dozen other Ukrainian regions overnight into Wednesday, killing at least 12 civilians, including three children, and wounding more than 40 in Moscow's latest devastating barrage, Ukrainian officials said.
Most of the dead were killed in a strike on apartment block in Pryluky in northern Ukraine

Ukraine had anticipated the attack, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warning the previous day that intelligence services had concluded that Russia was building up for a "massive" strike. He said Russia had fired 70 missiles and drones.
Although Ukraine knew about the looming attack, which coincided with Russian President Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday, it couldn't fend it off completely.

A Russian strike destroyed an apartment block in Pryluky, in Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region, killing nine people, including three children, and wounding 34, Interior Minister Ihor Vyhivskyi said.

In this photo provided by the Ukrainian Emergency Service, rescuers work on the scene of a building destroyed following recent Russian attacks in Pryluky on Wednesday. (Ukrainian Emergency Service/The Associated Press)
Deaths were also reported in three other Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv, according to Zelenskyy.
"The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively," the Ukrainian leader said on social media.

items: Why is it so difficult for Ukraine to take down Russia's jet-powered drones?

blocks.text: Ukraine is looking worldwide for available Patriot missiles, which are in short supply due to the Iran war.
"Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge. And air defence packages for us right now are a vital necessity," Zelenskyy said.
Russia says it targeted missile storage, production sites
In Kremenchuk, in the Poltava region, two people were killed and seven injured, said Vitalii Diakivnych, head of the regional military administration. A rescue operation was continuing.

"That is exactly what the enemy is counting on. For us to be afraid to fall asleep. To let our children out of our sight. To plan anything. So that everyone thinks: next time it could be my address," he said.
The children abducted by Putin’s war machine

Russia's Defence Ministry said the military carried out a massive strike overnight targeting industrial facilities involved in the production and storage of missiles and drones across Ukraine. Targets ‌included sites where the company Fire Point makes and stores Flamingo ⁠cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones in Kyiv, ‌as well as in the regions of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava and ​Kharkiv, it said.
The Current19:00On the ground in Ukraine as Russia ramps up attacks
The ministry said that port and ship repair facilities in the southern Odesa region and ships carrying cargo for the Ukrainian military were also hit.
Ukraine has hit back at Russia by launching long-range drones and missiles on oil refineries and storage depots.
Zelenskyy said Wednesday that Ukraine targeted two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions of Russia.
Russian officials made no immediate comment.

blocks.text: Zelenskyy also indicated that Ukraine had struck in the Black Sea. He posted images of a fire said to show an oil tanker burning in the water near the Russian city of Sochi.
It was not possible to independently verify the images.

The deaths and damage illustrated the difficulty Ukraine has in countering Russia's ballistic missiles and the new jet-powered drones used in Moscow's escalating bombardments. Without ammunition for its U.S.-made Patriot air defence systems, Ukraine can't stop Russian ballistic weapons. It is racing to develop a new generation of interceptors fast enough to catch Moscow's high-flying jet-propelled drones.
Escalating Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports is making shipping risky

Russia and Ukraine are engaged in a long-range aerial war as their armies remain largely deadlocked on the battlefield, more than 4½ years after Moscow's all-out invasion of its neighbour. The unrelenting aerial attacks are hurting Russia but could be ruinous for smaller Ukraine.
Putin is pressing ahead with the invasion in the belief that Ukrainians will buckle under the pressure and Kyiv's Western supporters won't stay the course, Western analysts say.

The European Commission on ‌Wednesday said it had disbursed €1.24 billion ($2 ​billion Cdn) to Ukraine ​to buy drones, drone interceptors, drone ​ammunition and ⁠missiles as ⁠part ‌of an earlier promised loan.

"Russia ⁠is pursuing a deliberate strategy of ‌terror. To protect people and infrastructure, Europe is ​stepping up. ⁠Others must step up ⁠their support too," ⁠European ⁠Commission ​President Ursula von der ​Leyen ⁠said in a statement.

articles.title: How did Christa Pike survive execution attempt - and what happens next?
articles.summary: The convicted killer of Colleen Slemmer is said to be awake and speaking in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections.
articles.byline: James FitzGerald, Kayla Epstein, Brandon Drenon

blocks.text: Watch: What we know about Christa Pike’s "unprecedented" recovery after failed execution
ByJames FitzGeraldKayla Epstein and Brandon Drenon
Convicted murderer Christa Pike has woken up and begun speaking from her hospital bed almost a week after authorities in the US state of Tennessee botched her execution, her lawyers said.
Pike, 50, was sent to hospital after surviving two attempts to execute her via lethal injection for the 1995 murder of a 19-year-old she met at a summer camp for troubled teens.
An independent review of what went wrong in the Nashville execution chamber on 30 September has been ordered by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee.
He has also halted executions in the state for the rest of the year.
Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressing
How did Pike survive?
The Tennessee Department of Correction is yet to say why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.

Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, says it was not the case that Pike had some "special immunity" but suggested it was simply that not enough of the drug pentobarbital reached her bloodstream to kill her.
Pike was injected with a second dose of the drug, according to the prison authorities' protocol, after the first did not kill her.
In interviews with the BBC, Zivot has suggested the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under Pike's skin than to have entered her bloodstream.
"Most of the pentobarbital, instead of circulating in her body, ended up in her arms, and that's how she lived," Zivot said.

Pike's medical condition of thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting condition, was highlighted in advance by Pike's legal team as an additional issue that could scupper the process. Before the attempted execution, they had filed a legal case challenging the injection protocol.
If clots of blood formed at the injection site as a result of thrombocytosis, they would potentially have blocked the chemical from entering her veins, the lawyers warned.

As the attempted execution took place, prison officials used at least seven needles on Pike during their efforts to establish intravenous (IV) lines, Pike's lawyers said afterwards. The woman could simultaneously be heard "crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly".
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who was murdered by Pike and her then-boyfriend, told NBC the failed execution had been "a mess".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her then-boyfriend

blocks.text: Image source, Family handout
Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her then-boyfriend
The Tennessee Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.

After it became clear that Pike was not going to die from the two doses, she was taken to hospital for life-saving treatment. States have a legal obligation not to deny medical treatment to prisoners.
What is pentobarbital?

Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.

Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.
The Tennessee correction department has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded".
But the department said the lethal injection chemical had "consistently been effective".
What happens next?
The full picture of Pike's current physical condition is unknown.

Although she was said to be awake and speaking in hospital as of 6 October, is it unclear whether she has any long-term health defects. Medical staff have been working to clear the drug from her body, a process that they expected to take about a week. She has been removed from a ventilator.
Zivot said Pike had been able to communicate in a "basic way", including by giving her name and making an incorrect attempt to guess the date.
Meanwhile she is reportedly handcuffed to her bed.
Watch: Witnesses recount Christa Pike's failed execution attempt
There is then the question of what happens to Pike next.

Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike, though executions in the state have been paused for the rest of the year. Meanwhile, it has been announced that the state's Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada is stepping down.
Pike's lawyers have made repeated calls for Lee, the state governor, to commute her sentence to the lesser punishment of life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.

In 2024, it allowed Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, using an experimental oxygen deprivation method, after their attempt to kill him by lethal injection failed two years earlier.
The Supreme Court has already been involved in Pike's case: it allowed the lethal injections to go ahead after a legal battle.
Has this happened before?
While there is a lengthy history of botched executions across the US, Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived after receiving a lethal injection.
Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, said she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike is conscious and speaking.
There had been seven previous cases in which prisoners survived slated executions, but in those cases, executioners were not able to inject anything into the inmates' veins, Denno told the BBC.
Pike "is the only person for whom some kind of toxin has been injected", she said.
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.

The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.
In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which does not take an ethical stance on the penalty.
What did Pike do? Who was Colleen Slemmer?
Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder a year earlier of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, which was perpetrated along with her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp.
Pike killed Slemmer at a camp for troubled teens, after accusing Slemmer of insulting her and attempting to steal Shipp from her.
Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder and showed them a piece of Slemmer's skull.

Shipp was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole and he remains in prison. He was spared the death penalty for his part in the attack because he was not yet legally an adult at the time.

Correction 1 October: This article originally referred to the inmate executed by the state of Louisiana in 1947 as Willie Smith. We have amended the article to make clear that his name was Willie Francis.

articles.title: [DECODED] What a fake Duterte tells us about our bigger AI problem
articles.summary: Disinformation spreads rapidly because it’s becoming easier and cheaper to create fakes, while the systems behind them are outpacing the safeguards meant to mitigate the risks

blocks.text: Disinformation spreads rapidly because it’s becoming easier and cheaper to create fakes, while the systems behind them are outpacing the safeguards meant to mitigate the risks

items: Lance Duterte is a synthetic online persona claiming to be related to former president Rodrigo Duterte, gaining significant social media attention despite being a creation of AI.
The persona has evolved over the years, with recent posts utilizing videos to enhance believability, highlighting the growing ease of creating fake identities online.

Concerns about the unchecked development of AI and its potential dangers have been raised by researchers and former employees in the field, emphasizing the need for safety standards similar to those in other industries.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Have you ever heard of a “Lance Duterte”? He’s a Facebook persona claiming to be a grandson of former president Rodrigo Duterte and the son of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Like his supposed family members, Lance has attracted a huge following on social media. He has over 382,000 followers on Facebook, and his posts rack up thousands of engagements each — many of which come from fans and supporters who gush over his conventionally attractive features. Some even tout him as a future celebrity or politician.
But as our researcher Alex Culla found out, Lance is not real. He’s a synthetic online persona made from AI.

When Alex pitched the story, I thought the name sounded familiar. Then I remembered: six years ago, I wrote a fact-check article about a Facebook account with the name “Lance Kurt Dong Duterte.” He falsely claimed that Tricia, daughter of former vice president Leni Robredo, sent a hate message to him via private message.

But this happened back in 2020, before consumer AI chatbots like ChatGPT became publicly accessible. And as Alex pointed out in her Decoded piece, the profile picture of the 2020 version of this persona looked different from the one currently active today.
So the persona has been around for years, but its posts today now include videos to make the lie appear more believable, thanks to the accessibility of AI.

Lance isn’t the first AI piece built around the Duterte name. Back in 2025, we also reported on how AI-generated images of Duterte statues were being shared by Facebook pages known for glorifying the Dutertes. These fakes were created a few months after the former president was arrested over a warrant issued by the International Criminal Court.
These things happen because it’s becoming easier and cheaper to create fakes, while the systems behind them are outpacing the safeguards meant to mitigate the risks.
Over the past week alone, news reports have quoted different AI researchers, employees, and former staff on the lack of safety culture in AI companies.

From OpenAI to Google DeepMind, current and former employees have expressed concerns about the risks of self-improving AI systems and warned that companies are doing too little to protect the world against AI’s potential dangers.

Another former OpenAI safety employee said that “the time for trial and error is over,” because AI capabilities have far outpaced the systems’ ability to act in ways that match human goals and values. He even argued that advanced AI systems should have safeguards in place comparable to those used in the nuclear power and aviation industries.

Even Anthropic, the company behind Claude, warned its potential IPO investors that AI could exhibit “self-preserving behaviors.” The company said in its IPO prospectus: “Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm.”

These warning bells echo concerns that advocates have long raised about social media. Cambridge Analytica whistleblower Chris Wylie once said that digital products should have moral standards and safety testing like those imposed on consumer goods. “We do not allow any other consumer product to just be released without any kind of safety standards,” Wylie said in a Rappler+ briefing back in 2023.
Three years later, we’re still grappling with the same concerns, now made worse by the unchecked development of AI.

Which is why Rappler built MUNI, a platform where facts and trusted voices can thrive. It’s a community space for verified information, where you can read news, chat with reporters, and talk with like-minded individuals who share your interests.

MUNI is not limited to Rappler. You can also find other newsgroups there, including Daily Guardian in Iloilo and SunStar in Cebu, so you can also join their chat rooms and take part in their discussions.
You can explore MUNI by downloading the Rappler app for free from the App Store or Play Store. MUNI is a tab on the Rappler app where you can join as many chat rooms as you want.

I encourage you to join the #EverydayTech channel on MUNI, where Rappler’s tech reporters host casual discussions about tech issues that matter every weekday at 10 am and 4 pm. We’d love for you to join the conversations! – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trump to speak to Putin about plague lab worker's death in Russia
articles.summary: Fears that the death may have been caused by pneumonic plague has prompted calls for more transparency from Russia.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has said he will speak with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin soon about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia.
"So far we are in very deep discussions," Trump said, adding that he would be able to report on his talks with Putin "probably" on Thursday.

Russian officials say they are investigating the cause of the 28-year-old's death. They say that those who came into contact with the victim all tested negative and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague - a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for transparency from Russia.

"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early.
People can be infected through:

items: infected flea bites
contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials
the inhalation of respiratory particles

blocks.text: Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm.
Reports first emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation in Siberia's Irkutsk region following the death.
The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier.

Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked - or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
But Russian officials have played down those reports. The country's health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology".
Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed.
The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death.
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was founded just over 100 years ago.

articles.title: Padilla, Go, others ask Supreme Court to restore 16-vote threshold
articles.summary: PDP-Laban party-aligned lawmakers and individuals have asked the Supreme Court to restore the mandatory 16-vote supermajority required to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Sens Robin Padilla, Bong Go, and Bato Dela Rosa, along with actor Philip Salvador during the filing of the certificate of candidacy on Oct. 4, 2025.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui
MANILA, Philippines — PDP-Laban party-aligned lawmakers and individuals have asked the Supreme Court to restore the mandatory 16-vote supermajority required to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.

In a petition for Certiorari and Prohibition filed on October 6, Sens. Robin Padilla and Bong Go, along with the Partido Demokratiko Pilipino-Lakas ng Bayan (PDP-Laban) and several lawyers, challenged the Senate Impeachment Court's September 23 ruling lowering the conviction threshold.

Joining Padilla, Go, and PDP-Laban as co-petitioners is former Energy Secretary Alfonso Cusi. Also included as co-petitioners are Israelito Torreon, Jimmy Bondoc, Ferdinand Topacio, Raul Lambino, Resci Angelli Rizada-Nolasco and actor Philip Salvador.

The petition names the Senate sitting as an impeachment court, presiding officer Francis Escudero, and the House of Representatives as respondents, while also seeking an urgent Status Quo Ante Order, Temporary Restraining Order (TRO), or Writ of Preliminary Injunction to halt the implementation of the new rule.

The petitioners maintained that the Constitution strictly requires a two-thirds vote — or at least 16 of the 24 sitting senators — to convict, and requested that any judgment rendered with fewer than 16 votes be declared void from the start and permanently prohibited.
“This case is not about whether the Vice President should be convicted or acquitted,” the petitioners, through the Law Firm of Torreon and Partners, said in a statement.

“It is about the number the Constitution requires before any conviction can lawfully be rendered. The Constitution says two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate. With twenty-four Senators, that is sixteen,” it added.

The Senate Impeachment Court’s ruling — adopted by a 13-1 vote with six senator-judges abstaining or absent — overturned a July 6 ruling by the Presiding Officer that maintained a fixed 16-vote threshold.
On September 30, the Supreme Court dismissed petitions challenging the Senate Impeachment Court’s interpretation of the two-thirds vote requirement needed to convict Duterte.
The high court dismissed the petitions for lack of standing and prematurity.

blocks.text: Royal Mail is to cut up to 2,500 jobs as the embattled company seeks to restructure its business amid intense competition and the continuing decline in letter deliveries.

The postal service, which has been fined a total of £37m since 2023 for missing delivery targets set by Ofcom, said the job cuts would focus on head office and “support function roles” with the restructure to be completed by the end of next year.

Pointing out that the volume of letter deliveries had declined more than 70% since their peak in the mid-00s, Royal Mail said the cuts would be achieved through “natural attrition” and a voluntary exit programme with no compulsory redundancies.

The company said there would be no reduction in operational frontline roles in delivery and processing, including the number of posties and drivers it employs. The cuts amount to less than 2% of Royal Mail’s workforce of more than 131,000.

“We have been working hard to reduce costs and simplify processes across all areas of the business as we transform to win in a very competitive market,” said Alistair Cochrane, the chief executive of Royal Mail. “These proposed changes remove duplication and allow us to invest further in the service we deliver for our customers.”

articles.title: Ferdinand Marcos Jr. unplugged: Why the President needs music
articles.summary: 'I’ve come to the conclusion that my life was lived with a soundtrack. When I hear a song, I remember when I first heard it, what I was doing, how I was feeling. Every big event in my life there was…

blocks.text: 'I’ve come to the conclusion that my life was lived with a soundtrack. When I hear a song, I remember when I first heard it, what I was doing, how I was feeling. Every big event in my life there was an accompanying track ongoing,' Marcos says in an interview with Gary Valenciano

items: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has a history of music-related controversies, including using a presidential helicopter to attend a Coldplay concert, which he described as 'unmissable.'
Marcos views music as an essential part of his life, associating significant events with specific songs and expressing admiration for the Filipino audience's enthusiasm for live performances.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Back in September 2024, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. had caused an uproar for hiring a band to play at his private birthday party.

While the Philippines is known as a music-loving country, it wasn’t just any band, that Marcos hired — it was acclaimed British pop-rock outfit Duran Duran, which was flown in just for his 67th birthday celebration.

But the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) had attested that the party, held at a Pasay City hotel, was thrown by “old friends,” and that the Duran Duran performance had merely come as a surprise to Marcos. Then-communications secretary Cesar Chavez had even told reporters in a message that the band’s appearance came “at no cost to the government.”
This wasn’t the President’s first music-related controversy, however.

Just a few months before that, in January 2024, the son of the former dictator had also found himself in hot water when the public caught wind of him using the presidential chopper to get to British band Coldplay’s concert at the Philippine Arena in Bulacan.

blocks.caption: Coldplay concert ‘unmissable’ for chopper-riding, ‘music lover’ Marcos

blocks.text: It was “unmissable,” he had told reporters in a chance interview several days after the show.
“It was, by the way, fantastic. Ask anybody who attended the concert. The show they performed was spectacular. I haven’t seen anything like it,” he said.
It seems, then, that the country’s biggest music fan happens to hold the state’s highest position. And Marcos was always one to make his affinity for music known.

Around the time of the 2022 presidential elections, an old clip of him playing the saxophone had gone viral. He had revealed in an interview with Gary Valenciano that premiered on October 5 that this, along with the flute, were instruments he had picked up in his youth. He had even gone on to join several orchestras.

blocks.caption: Ferdinand Marcos Jr. unplugged: Why the President needs music

blocks.text: Marcos had first studied music while he was pursuing his secondary education in England in the ’70s. He was a self-confessed troublemaker then, and was sent to his housemaster to receive his punishment.
“He said, ‘You’re here all the time. You’re always in trouble. Go find yourself a hobby so that you can occupy your time by doing something constructive,’” he recalled.

blocks.caption: Ferdinand Marcos Jr. unplugged: Why the President needs music

blocks.text: Back then, he had been listening to a lot of music anyway, so it only seemed like the natural choice. What had served as his musical awakening, he shared, was Lou Reed’s “Walk on the Wild Side,” which he had heard another student play out loud while he was making his rounds before class. Aside from playing the flute and the saxophone, he would later also study music theory.

“It’s a fascinating thing because unlike any other art form, music doesn’t exist anywhere else except in your brain. Think about it. A sculpture you can touch, a painting, you can look at and you can see the brushstrokes. All the other forms. This is just sound and it only becomes music because your brain interprets it as music. But the universality of it, everyone understands,” Marcos told Valenciano in the interview.
The President views music as an integral part of his life — as something he cannot live without. If anyone were to take it away from him, he tells Valenciano, he wouldn’t know how to manage.

“I just don’t know how I would get through the day,” he explained. “It’s the only thing that can change my mood. There are two things that can change my mood. Music’s one of them. The other one’s my children.”

Even Marcos’ big life events have specific songs associated with them. He and this art form have long been intertwined. “I’ve come to the conclusion that my life was lived with a soundtrack. When I hear a song, I remember when I first heard it, what I was doing, how I was feeling. Every big event in my life there was an accompanying track ongoing.”

But even as a big music fan, the President can’t seem to figure out why Filipinos excel so much at holding a note. He said that whenever his foreign friends would ask him why his countrymen were such good singers, he had never been able to give a proper answer.
Apparently, what he does know, though, is that Filipinos make the best concert audiences.

“I’ve heard it from Elton John, I’ve heard it from Sting. I’ve heard it from The Corrs. I’ve heard it from many of these artists that come. And they said, ‘The audience does all the work for me. I don’t have to sing. I don’t have to perform because the audience is singing for us,’” Marcos explained.

Most Filipinos are lauded for always enthusiastically singing the lyrics back to the performing artist as loud as they can. It’s become a big indication of who the Filipino people are as enjoyers of music.

In Marcos’ case, perhaps much of his repertoire as a music fan reflects in his willingness to do anything to catch his favorite bands perform live — even if it means flying a high-profile music act in for a private show or riding the presidential chopper to the Philippine Arena to beat the evening traffic, much to the ire of taxpayers. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sri Lanka's ex-first lady arrested over alleged misuse of children's hospital donations
articles.summary: The 73-year-old has been arrested over allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations.

blocks.text: Sri Lanka's former first lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa has been arrested over allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations raised for a children's hospital.
Anti-corruption authorities arrested the 73-year-old wife of former President Mahinda Rajapaksa at their Colombo home on Wednesday.

They are questioning her over the 10 million rupees ($30,300; £22,800) of donations collected by the Siriliya Saviya charity, meant to be spent on a specialised scanner for Colombo's Lady Ridgeway Children's Hospital.
But officials say such a scanner had already been donated by the Chinese government.
Shiranthi Rajapaksa has denied any wrongdoing and says the money has not been appropriated.
She returned to Sri Lanka on Monday from Singapore, where she was receiving medical treatment. She had filed a court petition to try to prevent her arrest, but the hearing was set for 12 October.
Ex-President Mahinda Rajapaksa's spokesperson, Manoj Gamage, has said the money is safe in Siriliya's accounts and that no fraud has occurred.

Mahinda Rajapaksa served as president of Sri Lanka from 2005 to 2015 and for years, his family held a tight grip over the country's politics. He was hailed by many as a hero for bringing an end to nearly three decades of civil war when Tamil Tiger rebels were crushed in 2009, during his first term as president.
But in 2022, protests broke out across the country as inflation surged and Sri Lanka ran out of fuel, food and medicine.
Mahinda's brother Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was serving as leader at that time, was eventually toppled.
Sri Lanka's current government, under President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, has since revived long-stalled corruption investigations involving various members of the Rajapaksa family.

Mahinda and Shiranthi's eldest son, Namal Rajapaksa, was arrested earlier this year over allegations linked to an aircraft procurement deal made during his father's presidency. He is currently held in remand.
His brother Yoshitha was also arrested earlier this year on corruption charges.

articles.title: Israelis mourn on anniversary of Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians grapple with war it sparked
articles.summary: Israelis gathered on Wednesday to commemorate the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack that killed 1,200 people, saw 251 taken hostage, and sparked a devastating war in Gaza that has left much of the…

image.caption: The family of Hilly Solomon visits her memorial photo and plaque at the Nova festival memorial site early Wednesday in Reim as Israel marks the third anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks. (Alexi Rosenfeld/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Israelis gathered on Wednesday to commemorate the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack that killed 1,200 people, saw 251 taken hostage, and sparked a devastating war in Gaza that has left much of the territory in ruins and its two million people living in dire conditions.

In southern Israel, families mourned at intersections, bomb shelters, and the site of a music festival that Hamas-led militants overran three years ago in the deadliest attack against Israel. It is the first anniversary that all the hostages are home, marking a new stage of grief.

For Palestinians, the anniversary brings another day of life of misery and difficulties after an Israeli retaliatory campaign in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of people. Most of the population of about two million people live in vast, squalid tent camps, with large parts of the strip's cities reduced to rubble.
More than half the territory remains in the hands of the Israeli military, and despite a ceasefire deal reached nearly a year ago, Israeli strikes continue almost daily.

items: 1 year since Oct. 7, the lives of these Israelis and Palestinians are forever changed
U.A.E. warned Netanyahu of major Hamas operation days before Oct. 7 attack: Israeli newspaper

blocks.text: For the region, the day highlights a startling transformation over the past three years. Israeli troops occupy a large chunk of southern Lebanon in their conflict with Hezbollah, which began firing on Israel in 2023 in support of Hamas.
Commuters in Tel Aviv conduct a moment of silence on the highway as part of a memorial ceremony on Wednesday. (Jack Guez/AFP/Getty Images)

Iran and the United States are locked in a confrontation that has seen attacks across Arab Gulf countries and has shaken the global economy — a conflict that Israel helped launch and that the Gaza war paved the way for even if they weren't directly connected.
Families mourn at music festival site

In Reim, the town where the music festival was underway on the day of the attack, families gathered around photos of their killed relatives. They hugged at 6:29 a.m. local time — the exact time the first rockets were launched three years ago — as booms from explosions in nearby Gaza were heard.
Anya Davitashili, who lost her 25-year-old son, Sean, said she comes to the site every Saturday because it's where she feels closest to him.
"I have a video of him dancing here that ends at 6:29 in the morning, it's in front of my eyes all the time," she said. "Every morning, you wake up and there is just endless missing."
Hundreds of people came to pay their respects to the more than 350 people killed in and around the festival site.
Released hostage marks 1st anniversary of freedom

Elkana Bohbot, 37, is marking the anniversary in Israel for the first time, after being released from 738 days of captivity last year. For most of that time, he said, he was held 50 metres underground in a dark, damp tunnel.
People attend a memorial service in Kibbutz Kfar Aza, southern Israel, where many community members were killed and abducted on Oct. 7, 2023. (Ariel Schalit/The Associated Press)

Bohbot, who was abducted from the Nova music festival , was kept in a small cell with other hostages, given very little food, and allowed to bathe only every few weeks, he said. His captors forced him to take part in several propaganda videos, including one where he acts out a fake call to his family.

In the 11 months since his release, Bohbot has undergone physical and emotional rehabilitation, written a book, begun a speaking career, travelled with his family, and celebrated all the holidays and birthdays he missed.
What Netanyahu knew before the Oct. 7 attacks
In August, his wife, Rivka, gave birth to a daughter, fulfilling a fierce promise that Bohbot made to himself in the tunnels to give his five-year-old son, Reem, a sibling.

The newborn Michele is "not a symbol for my people, she is more of a symbol for the enemy," Bohbot told The Associated Press. "So this child is the message for you that we were here, and we will always be here forever."
Palestinians struggle to recover in Gaza

No events are expected on Wednesday in Gaza, but Hamas in a statement praised the Oct. 7 attack as an example of "heroism, resilience and national solidarity" and said it had returned the Palestinian cause to the world's attention.
"The conflict with the enemy did not begin on that day, as its final chapters are not written yet," it said.
Palestinians in the territory said the extent to which their lives had deteriorated over the past three years was previously unimaginable.
"We witnessed death, destruction, and bombardment that we had never known before," said Walid Akram, a Gaza City resident who, like most in Gaza, has been displaced by the war.
Raed Khozeiq's coastal neighborhood in Tel al-Hawa was largely flattened. Nothing about his life now is the same, he said.
"No country in the world has gone through what we have experienced here," he said. "A war of extermination, starvation, the absence of schools and universities — nothing remains."

Israel's offensive has devastated the narrow strip and displaced around 90 per cent of its population, often multiple times. Restrictions on the entry of goods and aid have contributed to a severe hunger crisis.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Health Ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its figures but says around half were women and children. The numbers from the ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, are seen as generally reliable by UN agencies and independent experts.

While a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025 has halted the heaviest fighting, Israeli strikes have continued, targeting what Israel says are Hamas militants. Since the ceasefire, 1,460 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the ministry. Seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in that period.
Palestinians walk along a street in Gaza City on Tuesday, surrounded by buildings destroyed by Israeli military strikes in the Israel-Hamas war. (Jehad Alshrafi/The Associated Press)

Hamas portrayed the Oct. 7 attack as a response to decades of Israeli military occupation, land seizures and settlement construction. But the Palestinians' dream of an independent state appears even more distant.
Middle East altered

A contentious election in Israel at the end of the month hangs over this year's anniversary. The government's official memorial services took place on Oct. 5, closer to the Hebrew-calendar anniversary of the attack. The separate commemorations are indicative of the deep divisions over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's handling of the war and his reluctance to launch an official inquiry into failings of the day.

The attack set in motion a cascade of events that led to wars across the Middle East as Israel confronted Hamas, Hezbollah and their backer Iran. Israel has seized swaths of territory in Syria and Lebanon, where more than 300,000 Lebanese remain displaced.
The United States joined Israel in attacking Iran's military and nuclear program in two rounds, battering Iran and upending global markets far from the battlefield.
Violence has also risen across the Israeli-occupied West Bank, where Israel's far-right government has emboldened extremist settlers who have attacked Palestinians and destroyed their property.
