articles.title: Japan beer giants raided over alleged price-fixing cartel
articles.summary: Asahi and Kirin confirmed their premises were searched by Japanese competition authorities.

blocks.text: Japanese officials have raided the country's biggest beer makers over allegations they worked together to raise the price of their beverages.
Asahi and Kirin confirmed to the BBC their premises had been searched by the Japan Fair Trade Commission, adding that they would fully cooperate with the government authority.
There are reports Sapporo Breweries and Suntory Spirits were also raided. Both firms have been contacted for comment.
Asahi, Kirin and Sapporo all saw their share price fall after news of the investigation broke on Wednesday. Suntory is not publicly-listed.
According to the Japan Times, the investigation centres on the companies raising their prices in April last year and in October 2022.
All four companies announced increases, citing the rising cost of raw materials as well as other factors such as energy and transportation.
Kirin Holdings said its subsidiary, Kirin Brewery Company, was searched "on suspicion of a violation of the Antimonopoly Act".
It said it takes the matter "very seriously", adding it would "fully cooperate with the Japan Fair Trade Commission's investigation and any requests for cooperation".
Kirin Holdings said: "At present, the impact of this matter on the company's financial results has not been determined. The company will promptly disclose any material developments as they arise."

Asahi Breweries said it was "subject to investigation by the Japan Fair Trade Commission regarding a suspected violation of the Act on Prohibition of Private Monopolization and Maintenance of Fair Trade".
It added: "We will fully cooperate with the commission."
The Japan Fair Trade Commission has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: [In This Economy] Cesar Virata, technocrat who helped finance a dictatorship
articles.summary: How should we remember a capable technocrat who helped keep such a government going?

blocks.text: Cesar Virata, who died on October 2 at age 95, was a familiar presence at big events of the UP School of Economics, attending in his wheelchair.
That is the extent of my personal acquaintance with him. I did not know him closely, and I leave the intimate recollections to his family, friends, and colleagues.

He may well have been as wise and kind as those who knew him remember. On Facebook, I saw an outpouring of condolences from my friends for whom Virata was a tito (uncle/respectful title for an older person), ninong (godfather), mentor, friend. Those qualities deserve their place in the tributes and obituaries.
But Virata’s long service to the Marcos dictatorship deserves equally serious attention.

The fact is that Virata headed the finance department/ministry from 1970 to 1986 and served as prime minister from 1981 until the dictatorship fell. These were positions at the very heart of a government that, in the end, impoverished Filipinos and left the country with debts that outlived the regime.
How should we remember a capable technocrat who helped keep such a government going?

In my 2023 book False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, I discussed how Marcos’ technocrats helped make the regime’s massive foreign borrowing possible. Virata was a central figure in that group.

To the uninitiated, technocrats are officials whose authority rests on specialized expertise. Under Marcos, they included economic managers with advanced degrees and international connections, people who could speak the language of bankers and development institutions.

This mattered enormously for the Marcos dictatorship. Borrowing requires lenders willing to believe that you can repay. Officials like Virata helped present the Philippines as a country whose economy was being managed competently—even as political power became increasingly concentrated in the hands of the dictator and his cronies.

The technocrats’ credibility helped the regime obtain money from foreign banks and institutions such as the World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF). The backdrop is that the economic managers were confronted with the task of maintaining a fixed exchange rate and maintaining an ample supply of dollars. The borrowings, totaling more than $25 billion over the Marcos years, helped finance the government and prolonged its ability to operate.
In the book, I described this as effectively “deodorizing” the Martial Law regime. Technical competence gave international creditors reasons to keep dealing with a dictatorship.

Of course, the technocrats and Marcos’ cronies were often at odds. They were characterized once as separate if opposing spokes in a wheel, connected by the hub that was Marcos. Political scientist Teresa Encarnacion Tadem’s research documents how crony interests undermined Virata’s group, even as its relationships with international financial institutions strengthened its position within the government.

Those conflicts show the limits of the arrangement. Marcos retained the power to accommodate his cronies and disregard technical advice, while continuing to benefit from the credibility lent by his economic managers. Both groups could serve the same regime while disagreeing bitterly about its policies.

Eventually, some technocrats left one by one. Gerardo Sicat, for instance, left his position as director-general of the National Economic and Development Authority in 1981, just as the economy was tumbling into decline and crisis. Virata remained to hold the fort.

Many years later, Sicat would write a tome of a biography for Virata, titled: Cesar Virata: Life and Times Through Four Decades of Philippine Economic History. Published in 2014, it offers a sympathetic account of Virata’s predicament as the chief technocrat during the crisis years. As Hal Hill’s review explains, it portrays a reformer battling Imelda Marcos and the cronies, attempting to restrain spending, and eventually offering a resignation that Marcos refused.

But this defense leaves important questions unanswered. The disappearance of congressional opposition after Martial Law may have made economic reforms easier to implement. It also removed democratic checks on the borrowing and spending that helped bring the country to ruin. Economists should count those costs to our institutions as well.

As well, the unsuccessful offer to resign doesn’t erase the consequences of remaining in office. Virata’s credibility continued to help Marcos obtain foreign financing even as the regime’s abuses and economic failures became increasingly evident.

Truthful reminiscences of Virata’s life and times must acknowledge the fact that technocrats like him were crucial in propping up the dictatorship and the crony capitalism that flourished at that time.

Consider an admission by Virata himself that I quoted in False Nostalgia, drawing on economist James Boyce’s account. In 1984 Virata admitted, “We were quite liberal in guaranteeing loans,” referring to “behest loans” or loans that were granted by president Marcos to select friends and family members, obtained from government financial institutions.

Virata explained that some companies had been interested in making money from equipment purchases rather than operating the businesses those purchases were supposed to support. He called this “one of the major faults in our system.”

A loan guarantee is a promise to pay if the borrower cannot. It can help a worthwhile project obtain financing, but it also exposes the guarantor to losses. When public institutions extend guarantees too freely, as Virata admitted to doing, private business failures can become public financial obligations.

That is why Virata’s admission matters. It points to a gross failure in how the Marcos regime assessed and assumed financial risks. The public was left exposed to projects whose supposed developmental benefits might never materialize.

Indeed, state-owned banks like the Development Bank of the Philippines, and even the old Central Bank, were left with deteriorating balance sheets as it became impossible to collect the behest loans that they gave out to cronies. Rescuing crony businesses in the 1980s weakened the institutions financing them, which themselves needed rescuing. The costs, in short, spread far beyond the favored borrowers.

Then there’s the 1983 debt moratorium. In October that year, not long after senator Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr. was killed on the tarmac, Virata and then-Central Bank governor Jaime Laya had gone to New York to seek a 90-day moratorium on principal payments to private creditors. By that time, the country could no longer meet its debt obligations as scheduled.
The same government that had borrowed so heavily was now asking for more time to pay.

Sure, the Philippines faced a hostile international environment: higher global interest rates and the international debt crisis also battered other developing countries. Virata alone did not cause the Philippine crisis, and negotiating relief was necessary once the country was in trouble.

But decades of bad domestic decisions had made us weak and vulnerable. Foreign borrowing came with repayment obligations, and politically favored projects could fail to generate the income needed to meet them. In hindsight, therefore, economic managers must be assessed on the risks accumulated during their tenure alongside their efforts to manage the eventual collapse.

It didn’t help that Virata was tone-deaf about people’s increasing economic hardships. In a controversial interview in the June 1, 1984 issue of Mr & Ms Special Edition, Virata was quoted as saying, “Well, I do not know what they mean by crisis… They never had it so good.”
They never had it so good.

He argued that basic needs were being supplied and that people should not mistake the absence of luxuries for a crisis. Recall that this was months after the debt moratorium, amid an economic crisis aggravated by crony capitalism and reckless borrowing. In effect, Filipinos were paying for the failures of a government whose prime minister was assuring them that life had never been better.

Whatever his disagreements with Marcos behind closed doors, Virata was on record publicly defending the regime’s economic record. His own words complicate the picture of a technocrat merely trying to contain the damage.
There is a familiar defense of officials who stay under an abusive leader: they are supposed to have restrained the damage from within.
Sure, sometimes they do. But that defense still leaves a difficult question: How much did their continued service help the government survive and carry on with the very practices they opposed?

For economists like me, this is an uncomfortable question worth asking. Expertise gives us influence, but things get complicated when we lend that influence to institutions and political leaders with dodgy reputations. Technocratic competence can make a government more credible even when its use of power deserves public resistance. Recently, we’ve seen that play out as well in the dictatorial regime of Rodrigo Duterte—the subject of my second book, Twin Plagues.

In Virata’s case, complicity lies in his sustained role in financing and administering the dictatorship. He didn’t necessarily steal public money or order an abuse, but nobody can deny the responsibilities he held and the regime his work helped to sustain.

People can remember his kindness and generosity, and we sympathize with the family and friends. But the country as a whole must also never forget what happened under the government Virata willingly served for so long.

There have been stringent efforts to memorialize Virata in past years, like a biography written by Sicat as well as the 2013 renaming of the UP Diliman College of Business Administration (CBA) into the Cesar E.A. Virata School of Business or VSB (a highly contested move until now; many students and faculty still insist on calling their college the CBA rather than the VSB).

At any rate, Virata’s passing should at least prompt a fuller reckoning with his record as a public servant. His personal virtues belong in his obituary—but so does his complicity in the Marcos dictatorship. – Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD, is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics. His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. His second book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and COVID-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, was published by Penguin Random House SEA in June 2026. Follow him on Instagram (@jcpunongbayan).

articles.title: Suspected pneumonic plague in Siberia: What we know about the disease
articles.summary: After a worker at a Russian plague research institute in Siberia died October 2, 2026, nearly 200 of her contacts were under medical observation. But authorities there denied pneumonic plague had…

image.caption: The ECDC is closely monitoring the situation in Siberia after the death of a Russian laboratory workerImage: Britta Pedersen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: UPDATE: Following initial reports raising concerns that a lab worker had died accidentally of pneumonic plague, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said it was now also "closely monitoring the situation."

However, in a statement published October 6, 2026, the ECDC said that "based on the limited information currently available, there are no reports of secondary cases and no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission that would cause further spread of the disease."
What you need to know about plague

items: There are three forms of plague, all caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
The three forms of plague are bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.

Bubonic plague is the most common form; it does not spread from person to person. If untreated, the bacteria can move through the body and bloodstream, causing septicemic plague, which causes internal bleeding and organ failure.
If the bacteria reach the lungs, they cause pneumonic plague. Pneumonic plague is highly contagious because it can pass from person to person through the air, for example, via coughing.
If untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.

blocks.text: Speculation over the death in a Russian plague laboratory

Following the death of a Russian laboratory worker, there is speculation about an outbreak of pneumonic plague, a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs. Russia denies there is a broader risk to the community.

Russian officials have said the laboratory worker's death was not caused by a plague pathogen. The 28-year-old died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," according to Russia's Interfax news agency, citing Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's disease-control agency. According to that agency, samples taken from the woman showed no microorganisms "related to her professional activities." This contradicts earlier information.
Local media had previously reported that the woman, who worked at an institute dedicated to fighting plague, had dropped a test tube.
She reportedly died on Friday, October 2, 2026, at the district hospital in Shelekhov, a town near Irkutsk in Siberia.

According to official Russian figures, authorities placed two hospitals and a children's clinic under quarantine. Local reports said staff at the institute were being quarantined at their workplace. The US news site Axios has reported that around 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under observation. There were no further reported infections.
Russia rejects reports of plague in Siberia

Even so, distrust of how Russia handles information persists. On one of DW's Russian-language social media channels, a user wrote: "It wouldn't surprise me if this turns into a disaster now, both in terms of the spread and the quarantine measures."
Pneumonic plague: a fast-moving lung infection
All that is known for certain, at the time of writing and first publication (October 5, 2026), is that pneumonic plague is highly contagious.

Pneumonic plague is a form of plague that infects the lungs. Like every form of the disease, it is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals, such as rodents and in the fleas that feed on them.
The World Health Organization describes the pneumonic form as the most virulent type of plague.

Its incubation period can be as short as 24 hours, and it is the only form that passes easily from person to person through respiratory particles released when a sick patient coughs. This is why, according to the WHO, it can trigger severe epidemics.
Symptoms appear quickly: high fever, headache and weakness, followed by a rapidly worsening pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain and a cough that often brings up blood.
A person can catch pneumonic plague by breathing in the bacteria directly, or by developing it when bubonic and/or septicemic plague go untreated and spread to the lungs.
Could a Russia plague case trigger wider concern?
What is the difference between bubonic and pneumonic plague?
Pneumonic plague is not a separate disease. It is one of three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.
All are caused by the same bacterium.
What sets them apart is where the infection settles in the body, and that shapes how the disease spreads and how deadly it is.

Bubonic plague is the most common form and the one most people think of when they hear the word "plague." It usually follows a flea bite. The bacteria travel to the nearest lymph node, which swells into a painful lump known as a bubo. According to the WHO, it rarely spreads between people.

blocks.caption: The bacteria Yersenia pestis is responsible for the plagueImage: James Cavallini/BSIP/picture alliance

blocks.text: If bubonic plague goes untreated, the bacteria can move further through the body. If they spread into the bloodstream, the disease can become septicemic plague, which causes bleeding under the skin, tissue death in the fingers and toes, and organ failure. If the bacteria reach the lungs, the illness becomes pneumonic plague, the form that can pass from person to person through the air. Both septicemic and pneumonic plague can also develop directly, without a bubo appearing first.
Left untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.
Pneumonic plague treatment: antibiotics within the first 24 hours
Pneumonic plague is curable, but only if treatment starts quickly. The WHO warns that without treatment it can kill within 18 to 24 hours of the first symptoms.
Common antibiotics can cure the infection, and recovery rates are high when patients are treated within about a day of falling ill.

Speed is what decides the outcome. Doctors are advised not to wait for laboratory confirmation and to start antibiotics as soon as plague is suspected, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The drugs themselves are not rare or specialized. They are standard, widely used antibiotics, and patients usually need a course of up to two weeks. To stop the infection spreading, patients are kept in isolation, and wearing masks helps protect those around them, the WHO says.
Preventive antibiotics and isolation for close contacts

People close to a patient are treated as well, even if they have no symptoms. Both the WHO and the CDC recommend a seven-day course of preventive antibiotics for close contacts of anyone with pneumonic plague.
The WHO does not recommend a plague vaccine for the public. It reserves vaccination for high-risk groups, such as laboratory staff who work with the bacterium and health workers.

articles.title: California pair charged with abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children
articles.summary: Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang were arrested at their Arcadia mansion after 21 children were removed from their custody last year.

blocks.text: A California pair has been charged with multiple counts of abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children - some as young as two months old - and dissuading a witness.
"The number of children who were subjected to this alleged horrific abuse is unprecedented," Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan J Hochman said in a statement.
Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang, who US media describe as a couple, were arrested at their Arcadia mansion on Tuesday.
The pair pleaded not guilty at a Pasadena courthouse, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported.
Xuan, 66, and Zhang, 39, are accused of conspiring to subject 15 of the 16 children living in their home to repeated physical abuse, after 21 children were removed from their custody last year.

The pair ran their own surrogacy company and are accused of making false statements to at least two women who became surrogates, indicating that Zhang was struggling to conceive, according to the criminal complaint.
As of May 2025, Zhang maintained a spreadsheet that tracked 21 children, including those born to surrogates.
Officials said the investigation began that month when Zhang brought a two-month-old boy to the hospital with a head injury, telling medical staff that the baby had fallen from a bed.
The couple's lawyer Mitchell Krems said the allegation was a "mischaracterisation" based on the evidence he has reviewed, CBS News in Los Angeles reported.

Hospital staff informed law enforcement, and when police arrived at their home they discovered three different rooms called "learning centres" under the supervision of multiple nannies, which Hochman described as a "house of horrors".
The mansion allegedly had 32 motion-activated cameras which Hochman said were used by the couple to monitor the discipline given by the nannies.
Footage allegedly shows the nannies spanking, slapping or hitting the children.
One nanny, Chunmei Li, is accused of hitting the two-month-old baby who suffered the head injury two days before he was brought to the hospital.
Krems said Li was quickly fired, CBS News LA reported.

Li, 58, was previously charged with one felony count of child abuse under conditions likely to cause great bodily injury or death. Hochman said she was on the run with a $105,000 (£88,800) warrant for her arrest.
In July 2025, the couple's home was first raided by authorities, who took 21 children into state custody.
Arcadia Police Department said at the time the couple's house was first raided that the children ranged in age from two months to 13 years old, but most were between one and three years old.
Fifteen of the children were taken from the couple's home while six others were living elsewhere and also later taken into custody.
Krems said his client Xuan was innocent.
"He is being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family," CBS News quoted the lawyer as saying.
Investigators believe the surrogate mothers were from around the country and they were unaware they were carrying embryos for the couple at the same time.

Melissa Brisman, the attorney for two of the surrogates, told CBS News: "This is wonderful news that people will be held responsible for their actions and there will be consequences if you abuse the surrogacy system".
If convicted as charged, Xuan faces a possible maximum sentence of 17 years and four months in state prison, while Zhang faces up to 11 years and eight months. Li faces up to 12 years.

articles.title: NUJP slams Duterte lawyer over ‘unintended’ media intimidation
articles.summary: The group explained that the public’s right to be informed and the press’ freedom to report takes precedence over the interest of public officials whose transactions are under scrutiny.

blocks.text: Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte gestures as she arrives at the Hall of Justice in Quezon City, Metro Manila on Sept. 11, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — The National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) pushed back against one of Vice President Sara Duterte’s lawyers for insinuating during the impeachment trial that the media could face criminal liability for reporting suspicious financial transactions.

In a statement on Wednesday, October 7, the Filipino journalists’ union rejected an earlier warning from defense counsel Mark Vinluan regarding the potential imprisonment and fines that members of the media could face for violating certain provisions of the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001 (AMLA).

“A cursory reading of the Anti-Money Laundering Act’s (AMLA) penal provisions nor an apology for “unintended” intimidation can never curtail the media’s freedom to report on suspicious transactions and the corruption spearheaded by public officials,” the NUJP said.

During the impeachment trial on Monday, October 5, Vinluan brought up the confidentiality provisions of the AMLA while cross-examining Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Secretariat Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura.

The defense lawyer questioned Buenaventura about Section 9 of the AMLA, which prohibits officers of the AMLC and the media from disclosing information and contents about reported suspicious financial transactions.

Some senator-judges called out Vinluan on the same day for his "intimidating" remarks against the media and the Senate impeachment court, while on the next trial day, Vinluan apologized, saying it was not his intention to cause intimidation.
Public interest matters

The NUJP reiterated that the media is free to report on suspicious financial activities involving public officials that have been disclosed in official proceedings, as these become matters of public interest.
The group explained that the public’s right to be informed and the press’ freedom to report take precedence over the interests of public officials whose transactions are under scrutiny.
Section 16 of the AMLA, meanwhile, also states that the law cannot be used for political prosecution or harassment.
The group also stressed that they will not take attempts to intimidate journalists lightly, whether it is unintended or not.

“Public officials and their lawyers should know better than to wield the AMLA as a threat against journalists simply for doing their jobs,” the NUJP said. “The public has the right to know. The press will continue to report on matters of public interest.”

articles.title: Tito Sotto floats 'Tinikling' scheme using manager's checks
articles.summary: Senator-Judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III on Wednesday floated a supposed scheme wherein manager"s checks that are unutilized or have become stale are being returned to the issuing bank, possibly to…

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 5:31pm

Senator-Judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III on Wednesday floated a supposed scheme wherein manager’s checks that are unutilized or have become stale are being returned to the issuing bank, possibly to avoid audits.

This was revealed on the Day 35 of the impeachment trial, where witnesses from banks and financial firms were presented by the House prosecution panel to testify on Article 2 of the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte, alleging her unexplained wealth.

“I’d just like to ask if you’re familiar with the term used by my banker friend, who told me that ‘yun daw pag-issue ng manager’s check, pagkatapos hindi ginamit, later on after the 31st of December, ibabalik, ang tawag daw do’n ‘Tinikling,’” Sotto asked Marwin Galvez, division head for Central Manila branches of Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI).

(I’d just like to ask if you’re familiar with the term used by my banker friend, who told me that the practice of issuing a manager’s check, when it’s unused and is returned later after December 31st, is called Tinikling?)
“Gano’n daw ang ginagawa nung mga ibang umiiwas,” he added.
(That’s supposedly what some people do to evade something.)
The bank official said that he is not familiar with the term.
“Alam ko lang po ‘yung sayaw na Tinikling, Your Honor,” Galvez expressed.
(I only know the Tinikling dance, Your Honor.)

During the direct examination of Galvez, the prosecution flagged a P41.7 million worth of manager’s check linked to former president Rodrigo Duterte and VP Sara Duterte that was supposedly “floating” for years and was not being reflected in year-end balances.

Galvez confirmed the existence of such a joint peso time deposit opened on January 22, 2010, in the bank’s Julia Vargas Branch under the name “Rodrigo Roa Duterte or Rodrigo Roa Duterte and Sara Z. Duterte,” with a principal amount of P40,650,000.
He said that the time deposit had 12 rollover periods or renewals. At the last renewal in February 2011, he said the amount already increased to P41.7 million, including the interest.

In March 2011, the BPI official said a credit and debit memo showed that a manager’s check was purchased for P41.7 million. The manager’s check, however, remained unutilized after the validity period of six months.

Private prosecutor James Bryan Alih said that the prosecution intended to prove a "pattern," that a transaction in 2011 moved around for several more years and was later on used to purchase insurance policies.

“Ang punto lang naman po eventually is that ‘yung manager’s check na pinapaikot, hindi nakikita sa year-end balance kasi naka-float ‘yung pera na ‘yun. ‘Yun lang naman ‘yung gusto naming i-establish as a baseline,” Alih said.

(The only point is that the manager's check that is being circulated is not reflected in the year-end balance because the money is already floating. That's all we want to establish as a baseline.) — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Joint account of Sara, Rodrigo Duterte paid P16-M to Sammy Uy with manager's check -- witness
articles.summary: A joint bank account under the name of Vice President Sara Duterte and her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, was used to purchase a P16-million manager's check for businessman Sammy Uy, a…

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 5:26pm

A joint bank account under the name of Vice President Sara Duterte and her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, was used to purchase a P16-million manager's check for businessman Sammy Uy, a bank official said Wednesday.
Prosecution witness Marwin Galvez, division head for central Manila branches of Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI), testified on the matter on Day 35 of the impeachment trial of the vice president.
"Based on the records, we submitted your honor, the payee (beneficiary) po ng manager's check number 20536 dated May 30, 2016 is Samuel C. Uy," Galvez said.
Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV, a longtime critic of the Duterte family, has accused Sammy Uy of being a drug lord.
Trillanes had also previously alleged that the Duterte family, including the vice president, received P181 million from Sammy Uy.

Galvez also testified that two sets of time deposits under the names of the vice president and former president Duterte amounting to P41 million and P55 million were later used to purchase a manager's check worth P96 million. The elder Duterte was then listed as the payee for P41 million.

Upon inquiry of Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero, the BPI official said the amount in the purchase from the bank through a manager's check is not reflected in the ending balance of the account holder because it will be entered into the settlement account of the bank.
"Can the funds [stated in manager's check] be in limbo?" Escudero asked.

The BPI official replied, "Correct. Hangga't hindi po ibinabalik sa amin ng purchaser [ng manager's check [yung cheke], or in the case po of the payee, 'yung original [check], hindi po siya bumabalik sa account po ng bumili po."
(Unless the purchaser of the manager's check or the payee returns the manager's check to us, that will not reflect under the account of the purchaser of the manager's check.)

Senator judge Paolo Benigno "Bam" Aquino IV expressed surprise that such "scheme" is allowed given that it will allow an account holder to purchase a manager's check to prevent that amount from being reflected in the ending balance of the account holder.
Galvez said it was not uncommon.
Senator judge Panfilo Lacson's observation was more pointed.
"Without pre-empting the prosecution panel, may I venture. You (prosecution) are trying to establish a pattern and proving concealment," Lacson said.
Private prosecutor James Alih answered in the affirmative.

Defense counsel Michael Poa later argued said the vice president's signature was not seen in the application for manager's checks, and that he was told by his client that she was not aware of such transactions.

Asked by Senator-judge Hontiveros if that means that the vice president is putting the responsibility to her father, Poa said the vice president's point is limited to her being unaware of such manager's check purchases.
"Hindi po niya natatandaan... Wala siya naging participation (She does not remember... She has no participation in this)," Poa said. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Ronaldo stays on under cloud as Messi exits internationals
articles.summary: Just hours before Lionel Messi played his last match for Argentina, Cristiano Ronaldo posted his latest salvo in a row with Portugal. Ronaldo wants to play on despite the troubles, while Messi bathed…

image.caption: Cristiano Ronaldo did not get on the pitch against Norway so lef the Portugal squadImage: Grzegorz Wajda/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: They are the two players who have defined the last two decades. As football became ever more popular, commercial and dominant in the cultural and sporting landscape, Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi remained its twin peaks.

Along with that has come endless social media posts, stories and discussions about who is better. Does Messi's World Cup and two Copa America titles with Argentina trump Ronaldo's Euro 2016 win and two Nations League titles? Or does the Portuguese's greater number of goals mean more? How about their club honors?
It is, essentially, a subjective argument and not one that can ever be resolved. It remains to be seen whether that's also true of the public spat between Ronaldo and his Portugal coach Jorge Jesus.

On Tuesday, Messi scored a 126th goal in his 208th game for Argentina. Shortly before he did, Ronaldo posted a 2,000-word statement in which he stopped short of quitting the national team but said there was an "absolute breakdown of trust" between him and the coach.
'There will be time' for Ronaldo's Portugal farewell

Ronaldo's comments refer to Portugal's recent match against Norway in which he said he was initially to be rested before being asked to warm up as a substitute without ever being brought on. The striker, 41, walked away from the team's camp for the remainder of the international break, but said the story is not over.

"I can promise all my fans, and naturally especially all Portuguese people, that we will have one or more farewell matches. There will be time for that," said Ronaldo, who plays for Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

"Despite the absolute breach of trust in the coach's word, as anyone who witnessed these conversations can attest, I should not have done it," Ronaldo said. "The responsibility is entirely mine. I apologize to the Portuguese people once again, but the breaking of one's word has, for me, a defining impact.

blocks.caption: Ronaldo and Messi were, arguably, at their peaks when playing for Spanish giants Real Madrid and Barcelona in the mid 2010sImage: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "I felt that, from that point on, my staying would only harm the group, and I did what I have always said I would do if I didn't feel useful: I picked up my bags and left," he continued before suggesting he accepted there may be a need for the coach or federation to punish him.
Messi: Argentina exit 'deeply painful'
It was a long way from the emotional scenes in Rosario, Argentina. Instead of anger and recrimination, the overriding emotions there were gratitude, nostalgia and sadness.

"Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I'd like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you," Messi, who now plays his club football for Inter Miami in the US, told the 80,000 fans who had packed in to see him score a penalty in a 3-0 win over Benin.

For some, the contrasting evenings offered a neat synopsis of the pair. Ronaldo, less naturally gifted than his counterpart, has made the most of his talents with a singular focus which many believe often makes him prioritize himself over the team. He has had similar fallouts with managers and head coaches before, including Jose Mourinho at Real Madrid, Erik ten Hag at Manchester United and Portugal's 2022 World Cup coach, Fernando Santos.
Ronaldo has 100 goals in his sights
Ronaldo's much-discussed aim to reach 1,000 career goals is held up by some as further evidence of where his motivations lie.

"You know what my goal is. I want to win trophies, and I want to reach that number (1,000 goals) that you all know. I will reach the number for sure, if no injuries," he said last December. He is currently on 979.

For others, that is simply what is required to be the best. While Messi's quiet character and general refusal to play out his life in public suggest a more humble character focused on helping the team, his genius has undoubtedly changed the teams around him. In the 2026 World Cup, he barely broke into a run but still led an otherwise fairly limited Argentina to the final with eight goals.

There will be no more Messi goals for Argentina and, despite his promises, no absolute assurances that the world will see Ronaldo in a Portugal shirt again. For now, both will head back to their club sides to play out their twilight years away from the intensity of Europe's top leagues. But wherever they go from here, the spotlight will keep following.

articles.title: Underground AI cybercrime tools surge in 2026
articles.summary: AI is making phishing, voice scams, identity fraud, and malware development cheaper and easier to scale, while lowering the technical barrier for cybercriminals

blocks.text: AI is making phishing, voice scams, identity fraud, and malware development cheaper and easier to scale, while lowering the technical barrier for cybercriminals

items: Artificial intelligence is making cybercrime tools more accessible, enabling less-skilled attackers to engage in phishing, identity fraud, and malware development.
AI is enhancing the capabilities of cybercriminals, allowing them to conduct sophisticated attacks.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Artificial intelligence is making cybercrime tools cheaper, easier to use, and more widely available, helping less-skilled attackers carry out phishing, identity fraud, and malware development at greater scale, according to research from the US-based Halcyon Ransomware Research Center.

Halcyon tracked nearly 4,000 posts across 77 Telegram channels, 20 dark web forums, and five underground markets between October 2025 and May 2026. It found that messages advertising AI-related cybercrime tools rose from fewer than 50 per month in late 2025 to more than 1,400 by February 2026.

The researchers said the underground market had rapidly developed many of the features of legitimate software businesses, including subscriptions, free tiers, automated storefronts, and multi-platform distribution.

Halcyon grouped the tools into four categories: weaponized large language models (LLMs), AI-enabled identity fraud, AI-assisted malware and attack infrastructure, and jailbroken or stolen AI services.

One of the biggest changes is the reduced technical barrier to carrying out attacks. “AI supplies skills [would-be hackers] never had. The results are often cruder (two ransomware crews have accidentally built malware they could not decrypt), but some capability beats none, and each tool for sale lowers the bar further,” Halcyon said.

AI tools can generate phishing messages, malicious code, and fraud scripts, while also helping attackers work in languages they may not speak. Halcyon said this allows inexperienced actors to perform tasks that previously required stronger technical skills, language ability, or operational experience.

In one striking example, Halcyon identified an AI-powered outbound call center advertised on a Russian-language hacker forum that could make up to 120 calls at the same time and communicate in as many as 25 languages. Operators could upload victim names and contact details through spreadsheets, while the system could address targets by name, generate human-like call center sounds, and provide live transcripts through Telegram and a web dashboard.

The researchers said the system represents a shift from AI being used mainly to generate written phishing content to conducting live conversations over professional telephony systems. This has resulted in some successful attacks. “One deepfake Zoom call resulted in a Singapore firm losing $499,000. A European energy company lost $25 million from a single cloned CFO voice,” Halcyon said.

Voice cloning adds another risk. Halcyon said some voice-cloning technology can reproduce a person’s voice using as little as three seconds of audio, making it easier for attackers to impersonate executives, employees, relatives, or other trusted contacts.

Halcyon found vendors selling deepfake video, voice editing, synthetic documents, and tools designed to bypass identity verification systems used by banks and online platforms. Some vendors advertised deepfake services that could generate head movements, facial expressions, and other responses intended to defeat “liveness” checks during online verification.

blocks.caption: Cybersecurity at ‘machine speed’: AI accelerates both attacks and defenses

blocks.text: AI is also accelerating malware development. Halcyon documented one malware framework containing about 88,000 lines of functional code that a vendor said had been produced in less than a week using an AI development assistant — work that without AI would have taken a professional team months to create.

However, Halcyon said it did not find evidence of criminals selling AI systems capable of independently carrying out fully autonomous cyberattacks. It did not observe tools explicitly advertising AI-powered “polymorphic” malware that could rewrite itself to evade signature-based detection, suggesting that some of the most advanced AI attack capabilities remain more theoretical than commercially available in the underground market.
But Halcyon warned: “Given the underground market demand for such a capability, we assess it is a matter of when, not if, such tools become available.”

Stolen accounts for popular services such as ChatGPT and jailbreak prompts meant to defeat guardrails were also being sold at very low prices, with the median price for stolen or jailbroken services at around $0.10.

What can people and organizations do? Halcyon said we can no longer rely on traditional phishing warning signs, such as poor grammar, awkward phrasing, and generic greetings, as AI-generated messages become more fluent and contextually appropriate.

It recommended that organizations shift from relying mainly on the content of messages to looking at behavior and verification patterns. These include unusual transaction requests, unexpected credential demands, and deviations from normal communication procedures.

With the rise of sophisticated video and audio phishing, Halcyon also recommended mandatory “out-of-band verification” for sensitive requests, wherein confirmation of a request is made through a separate communication channel from the one where the request came in.
Security teams should also prepare for a higher volume of attacks from less-skilled operators.

The researchers said AI has not created fundamentally new forms of cybercrime. Instead, it is reducing the time, cost, and expertise needed to carry out existing attacks while allowing criminals to operate at greater scale. – Rappler.com

articles.title: French police suspend use of stun grenades after high-school protester loses hand
articles.summary: Minister says use of grenades has been stopped ‘until we know what happened’ as protests across France continue

blocks.text: France is suspending the use of stun grenades by police at high-school demonstrations, the interior minister has said, amid mounting accusations of police brutality during a fortnight of protests marred by often violent clashes that have injured hundreds.

Laurent Nuñez told RTL radio on Wednesday that he had ordered a temporary halt to the use of the grenades “in the context of the high-school students’ movement” after a 15-year-old lost a hand during a protest in Lens, northern Fance, on Monday.

Authorities have not confirmed the exact circumstances – in particular, whether the boy had picked the grenade up or had been struck by it – but said up to 200 protesters had been hurling projectiles at police when the riot squad intervened.
Nuñez said he was suspending use of the grenades “until we know exactly what happened”.

The boy’s mother said on Wednesday that her son’s hand had been amputated. She told BFMTV: “His life has been stolen. He’s a 15-year-old kid, how can children be treated like that?” She said her son had not tried to pick the grenade up.

At least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff have been injured since the start of the protests over chronic teacher shortages, crowded classes, dilapidated buildings and long school days. About 750 police offers have also been wounded.

Nuñez said 18 internal police investigations have been launched over allegations of brutality during the demonstrations, including incidents in which young protesters have lost multiple teeth and one lost the use of an eye.

blocks.caption: Protesters battle teargas during demonstrations in Paris. Photograph: Véronique de Viguerie/Getty Images

blocks.text: He said inquiries were always opened over accusations of “non-proportional” policing, but insisted officers were there to protect the students. Rights groups and trades unions have repeatedly accused the police of using unnecessary force.

The decision came a day after at least 250,000 pupils, parents, teachers and unionists took to the streets in cities across France on the biggest day yet of the campaign, prompting the president, Emmanuel Macron, to hold an emergency cabinet meeting.

Most marches passed off without serious incident, but some – including in Paris – ended in sporadic vandalism and running skirmishes with riot police, with officers firing teargas and carrying out baton charges to disperse protesters.

The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, is due to make a speech on Wednesday on the demonstrations as well as the dire state of the country’s finances, which is severely constraining the government’s capacity to act on the protesters’ demands.
Lecornu on Tuesday condemned the violence and told parliament it could not be tolerated, while also rejecting accusations that the government had ordered “police repression” against the protesters.

Over the past fortnight demonstrators have set dustbins on fire outside their schools, destroyed bus shelters and hurled projectiles at riot police, who have responded with batons, teargas and riot-control rounds.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Police and students face off outside Sciences Po in Paris. Photograph: Tom Nicholson/Getty Images

blocks.text: Twenty-four schools have been burned or ransacked, while more than 6,500 people have ​been arrested, almost all of them minors. More than 1,800 are being prosecuted, nearly 1,500 of them under 18, the justice ministry has said.

Anne Savinel-Barras, the president of Amnesty France, said earlier this week that images and testimony from the protests “raise alarming concerns about the dangerous use of teargas, batons and policing techniques”.

The education ministry said classes had been wholly or partially suspended in 528 of the country’s 3,700 lycées – high schools attended by pupils aged between 15 and 18 – on Wednesday, a significantly lower number than on Tuesday.

The protests, months before key presidential elections to choose Macron’s successor, have rattled a government trying to reduce a ballooning budget deficit amid mounting investor concern over France’s ​sky-high debt and weak economic growth.

They have also sparked a heated political row, with the government accusing the radical-left La France Insoumise party of encouraging and even orchestrating the movement after numerous LFI MPs attended school blockades.
The party’s veteran leader and presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has strongly supported the protests, while urging non-violence.

articles.title: Leviste must return to PH, submit himself to court --DOJ
articles.summary: Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida on Wednesday said Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste must return to the Philippines and submit himself to the court"s jurisdiction following the issuance of an…

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 4:58pm

Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida on Wednesday said Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste must return to the Philippines and submit himself to the court’s jurisdiction following the issuance of an arrest warrant against him.
“He needs to submit to the jurisdiction of the court. So, kailangan siya umuwi (he needs to return),” Vida said in an ambush interview when asked how Leviste will post bail.
Vida said that refusal to listen to the court’s directive is disrespectful to the justice system.
“Kasi kapag hindi tayo sumunod sa utos ng korte, binabastos natin ‘yung sistema… ang batas natin kapag may arrest warrant, respetuhin natin at igalang natin ang kapangyarihan ng Korte,” he said.
(Because if we do not follow the court’s order, we are disrespecting the system… under our law, when there is an arrest warrant, we should respect it and respect the authority of the Court.)
“Ang panawagan ko bilang Secretary of Justice… lalo na sa kanya kasi may arrest warrant, sundin natin ang kautusan ng korte,” he added.
(My appeal as Secretary of Justice… especially to him because there is an arrest warrant, let us follow the court’s order.)
Earlier, a Makati regional trial court issued an arrest warrant against Leviste over an alleged violation of the Public Service Act.
Leviste is in France taking care of his mother, Senator Loren Legarda, who is on medical leave, La Viña said last September 25.
The congressman cannot post bail while abroad or before Philippine embassies, according to Vida.
Meanwhile, Vida said two of Leviste’s co-accused has posted bail.

In an interview on Balitanghali, Leviste’s spokesperson, Tony La Viña, said that he believes the accused must personally appear before the court when asked if an individual can post bail while abroad.
“Ang alam ko kailangan sa piyansa personal ka pumunta para mag bail,” he said.
(As far as I know, you need to personally appear to post bail.)
La Viña also said that they will file a motion in connection to the arrest warrant issued against him.

“May mga lawyers… mag file ng mga motion today related to the case para naman ma-lift ‘yung arrest warrant o ano,” lawyer Tony La Vîna, the spokesperson of Levista and Senator Loren Legarda, said on Balitanghali.
(There are lawyers who will file motions today related to the case so that the arrest warrant can be lifted.)
Leviste earlier said the Energy Department's allegations against him are baseless and a threat to public entities, including media organizations. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Nobelitis — How winning a Nobel Prize can give you delusions of grandeur
articles.summary: After being chosen for one of the world's most prestigious awards, some Nobel laureates lose touch with reality and suddenly start spouting unscientific nonsense. They're afflicted by what some have…

image.caption: Winning the Nobel Prize can go to anyone's head — James Watson, who was honored in 1962, is a prime exampleImage: Ivan Sekretarev/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Linus Pauling won not one, but two Nobel Prizes — the first, for chemistry, in 1954 for his research into the nature of the chemical bond, and the Peace Prize in 1962 for his work in the anti-nuclear weapons movement.

The American chemist not only won two Nobel Prizes, but won them on his own, a rare feat for any scientist. Such an honor often turns laureates into global superstars overnight, with millions hanging on their every word.
Nobel laureates can fall victim to Nobelitis

That instant fame can be dangerous, said Nils Hansson, a professor in the Department of History, Theory and Ethics of Medicine at Heinrich Heine University in Düsseldorf. Especially, he said, when these world-renowned experts "start spreading crazy, unproven scientific theories" — ideas that, when disseminated by Nobel laureates, risk being taken seriously.

That's what happened with Pauling. Beginning in the mid 1960s he began claiming that vitamin C was a universal remedy, a cure for everything from cancer to cardiovascular conditions and degenerative diseases like Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis or osteoarthritis.

Pauling developed an alternative treatment he called orthomolecular medicine, based on specific doses of vitamins and minerals for each patient. To this day, some 60 years later, evidence for his methods remains inconclusive.

Pauling's case is a classic example of "Nobelitis," or "Nobel disease" — not an official diagnosis, but an informal term used to describe how some laureates begin to suffer delusions of grandeur later in life. It was first coined by Paul Nurse, president of The Royal Society, the UK's national academy of sciences, and himself a winner of the Nobel Prize.
'Be skeptical of everything'

"Be skeptical of everything, including yourself and your own ideas," Nurse said in a 2019 interview with KU Leuven University in Belgium, when asked what made someone a good scientist. In cases of Nobelitis, that self-skepticism is the first to go.

blocks.caption: French virologist Luc Montagnier claimed COVID was created in a lab with parts of the HIV genetic code — 'utter nonsense,' according to virologist Christian DrostenImage: Mourad Balti Touati/ANSA/picture alliance

blocks.text: That was also the case with virologist Luc Montagnier, who was jointly honored in 2008 for his discovery of the human immunodeficiency virus, HIV, with colleague Francoise Barre-Sinoussi in the early 1980s.

Montagnier would later go on to support homeopathic medicine, another alternative treatment of disease and claim that HIV transmission in Africa could be diminished through better hygiene and nutrition.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Montagnier said the SARS-CoV-2 virus had been created in a lab with parts of the HIV genetic code. "It's difficult for a practicing virologist to say that a Nobel laureate in virology is spreading nonsense," said German virologist Christian Drosten on NDR's Coronavirus Update podcast in May 2020. "But that is utter nonsense."

James Watson, who was never known for his modesty, also let fame go to his head. In 1962, he was awarded the Nobel Prize along with Maurice Wilkins and Francis Crick for their discovery of the structure of the DNA molecule. But in the early 2000s, Watson repeatedly spread racist theories that Black people were less intelligent than white people.
For medical historian Hansson, Watson is a prime example that the Nobel Prize is not automatically awarded to a person who should be considered as a role model.
"You may have made a fantastic discovery, but that doesn't make you a universal genius," he said.
Even Noble Prize winners need to be challenged

But the great expectations of an admiring public may also contribute to the development of Nobelitis. Paul Nurse, who won the Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine in 2001, soon found himself getting daily requests for interviews on all sorts of topics.
"As if suddenly I was acknowledgeable about all workings of the world and of human beings," he told DW.

Nurse had this advice for researchers: "Be careful quite what you say. Talk about things that you do know something about that would be fine. And if you don't know so much or you're not sure about something, be really clear that you're not sure."
Homeopathy myths exposed
Hansson has also noticed that the media eagerly report whatever Nobel laureates say — even when prize winners stray far from their area of expertise.

Nobelitis sufferers are leaders in their fields, and rightly honored for their work with the Nobel. But they're also regular individuals, not immune to megalomania and other behavioral problems — meaning that homeopathy, orthomolecular medicine and other pseudosciences don't automatically become credible just because they're backed by a Nobel Prize winner.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Palace: Politicking? Probe into Gracioso claims must push through
articles.summary: The probe into the claims of former police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. must still continue despite accusations of politicking, according to a Palace official on Wednesday.
articles.byline: JEAN MANGALUZ, JONATHAN ANDAL, GMA News

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 4:39pm
The probe into the claims of former police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. must still continue despite accusations of politicking, according to a Palace official on Wednesday.
Vice President Sara Duterte slammed the accusations of Gracioso, an alleged ex-aide of former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco, saying that the former cop was paid off to make such claims.

“Kahit sabihin pa nila na ito ay pamumulitika at ‘yun naman ang kanilang tanging depensa, hindi dapat na matigil ang sinuman sa pag-iimbestiga patungkol sa issue na ito,” Undersecretary Claire Castro said during a press conference in Singapore.
(Even if it is said that this is politicking, and that is always their defense, no one should stop the investigation into this issue.)

Asked as to how credible Gracioso’s claims are, Castro said that whoever has the evidence is also the one with credibility. She also cited Ramil Madriaga, a former aide linked to Duterte, as an example.
Despite Duterte claiming that she did not know who Madriaga was, the former aide was able to show a video of the Vice President greeting him on his birthday.
Likewise, Castro said that Gracioso was able to show photographic proof that he has met with Duterte and Velasco.
“At ang pag-iimbestiga rin dito ay dapat na mas maging malalim, hindi para kung kanino man, kundi para ito sa taumbayan dahil ang pinag-uusapan dito ay pondo ng bayan,” Castro said.
(The investigation here needs to be deeper, not just for anyone, but for the people, because we are talking about public finds here.)
Gracioso claimed to have delivered around P2 billion to Duterte upon Velasco’s instruction. He also claimed to have bought Duterte gifts more than 20 times.
The Vice President said she does not know Gracioso Jr, and neither did she receive money from him.
The dismissed cop also claimed to have made deliveries to former president Rodrigo Duterte and to Davao representative Paolo Duterte.

The claim that suitcases containing cash were delivered to the Duterte family is a “fabricated story” to oust and disqualify Vice President Sara Duterte in the 2028 elections, former presidential spokesperson Salvador Panelo said.
The camp of Velasco on Saturday issued a statement on what it called “fabricated attacks” against him, saying the allegations have “no basis.”
Follow facebook.com/gmanewsonline for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: DepEd set to roll out ARAL for mathematics
articles.summary: Grades 1 to 10 students assessed to be ‘not proficient’ or ‘low proficient’ in numeracy are the target participants of the ARAL Mathematics program

blocks.text: CLASS ONGOING. Students of Santolan Elementary School in Pasig City attend class on August 12, 2026.
Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring/Rappler
Grades 1 to 10 students assessed to be ‘not proficient’ or ‘low proficient’ in numeracy are the target participants of the ARAL Mathematics program

items: The Department of Education will introduce mathematics tutorials in its ARAL Program starting in school year 2026-2027.
The ARAL Mathematics program aims to provide targeted and flexible support to students.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Education (DepEd) will start to include tutorials for mathematics in its Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning or ARAL Program in school year (SY) 2026-2027.

Grades 1 to 10 students assessed to be “not proficient” or “low proficient” in numeracy are the target participants of the DepEd’s learning intervention program for mathematics, as they still need substantial guidance and support.

“The latest PISA (Programme for International Student Assessment) results showed us that real progress is possible when we focus on foundational skills, but it also served as a clear reminder of how much ground we still need to cover,” Education Secretary Sonny Angara said in a news release on Wednesday, October 7.

“With ARAL Mathematics, our goal is simple: to reach every learner, wherever they are in their learning journey. Whether a child needs help recognizing basic numbers or mastering algebraic concepts, we are building a system that gives them targeted, flexible support so no learner gets left behind.”

The implementation of the ARAL Mathematics program will start in Term 2 or “once schools are fully prepared and ready,” considering the availability of personnel, learning resources, and other implementation requirements, according to DepEd Memorandum No. 60 dated September 28.
The DepEd said the program, which will follow a self-paced approach, can be conducted using face-to-face, online, or blended learning sessions.

Students may be pulled out from their regular classes to participate in math tutorials or attend the sessions during off-school hours or weekends. Each session would run for an hour if held during weekdays, or two hours if during weekends.
A maximum tutor-to-student ratio of 1:15 must also be observed.

The PISA 2025 results showed that the Philippines posted an average score of 371 in mathematics, which was up by 16 points from the 2022 cycle. The country ranked 74th out of 90 countries in mathematics last year, an improvement from its previous ranking in the bottom 10.
But the global assessment also showed that 78.9% of 15-year-old Filipino students did not meet the minimum proficiency level for mathematics in 2025.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, which administers PISA, explains that students with minimum mathematics proficiency skills can “interpret and recognize, without direct instructions, how a simple situation can be represented mathematically (e.g. comparing the total distance across two alternative routes, or converting prices into a different currency).”

The ARAL Program, institutionalized through Republic Act No. 12028 in October 2024, seeks to help public school students who struggle in reading, mathematics, and science, as a way to address the country’s learning crisis.
The DepEd started the ARAL Program in SY 2025-2026, but only for reading. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Shell expects refineries to almost double the profit from every barrel of fuel made
articles.summary:
Record prices caused by global shortages amid shutdown of war-damaged refineries in Middle East and Russia

Shell’s refineries are expected to make almost double the profit from every barrel…

blocks.text: Shell’s refineries are expected to make almost double the profit from every barrel of fuel produced owing to record prices caused by shortages around the world.

In a market trading update on Wednesday, the energy supermajor forecast profit margins of $42 a barrel in the July to September period, far above the $24 a barrel of the second quarter and the previous high of about $28 in mid-2022.

The margins reflect the steep increase in the price of refined fuels, including diesel, relative to the cost of crude oil, as the shutdown of war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia squeezes supplies.

The Middle East crisis helped Europe’s biggest oil and gas company to a profit of almost $10bn (£7.5bn) for the second quarter of 2026, more than double the figure for the same period last year and its second highest quarterly earnings on record.
The market value of Shell, now the second largest company on the UK’s FTSE 100 index, climbed to a record high of £36.23 a share at the end of last month.

That share price was reached despite oil prices retreating from their 2026 peak of above $115 a barrel in spring to about $100. It was lifted by European gas prices, which doubled from the previous year over the summer, and record high diesel prices.

Global oil prices were slightly lower in the third quarter of the year. Brent crude averaged $85.60 a barrel, compared with $97.05 in the second quarter, but still well above the $68.14 recorded in the third quarter last year.
The diesel price premium over the global oil benchmark jumped above $100 a barrel for the first time, indicating record high profits from refining crude into fuels.
Shell operates some of Europe’s largest refineries alongside the French energy company TotalEnergies, which has the continent’s largest refining capacity.
TotalEnergies’ chief executive, Patrick Pouyanné, welcomed the opportunities created by the global energy crisis.

He told an industry conference in London this week: “We’re doing really well by being integrated. Integration means your refineries in Europe, which you thought were liabilities, are suddenly becoming goldmines.”
after newsletter promotion

Europe’s benchmark gas price index more than doubled to €70.50 (£60) in August. The price of gas reached an average of more than €48 a megawatt-hour in the second quarter before leaping to almost €64/MWh in the third quarter.

Shell’s gas production has been hard-hit by the Iran crisis, which led to severe damage to one of its key gas processing facilities in the Gulf, cutting its prewar gas production of 900,000 barrels ⁠of oil ​equivalent ‌per day (BOED) by a third.

Shell said on Wednesday that it expects gas production to climb to about 740,000 to 780,000 barrels ⁠of oil ​equivalent ‌per day, ‌up sharply from its previous forecast of 570,000 to 630,000 BOED for the quarter. It produced about 631,000 BOED in the second quarter.

articles.title: Prosecution flags 'floating' P41.7-M manager's check linked to Rodrigo, Sara Duterte
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel on Wednesday flagged a P41.7-million worth of manager"s check linked to former president Rodrigo Duterte and Vice President Sara Duterte that was supposedly “floating” for…

blocks.text: The House prosecution panel on Wednesday flagged a P41.7-million worth of manager’s check linked to former president Rodrigo Duterte and Vice President Sara Duterte that was supposedly “floating” for years and was not being reflected in year-end balances.

On Day 35 of the impeachment trial, Marwin Galvez, division head for Central Manila branches of Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI), confirmed the existence of a joint peso time deposit opened on January 22, 2010, in the bank’s Julia Vargas Branch under the name “Rodrigo Roa Duterte or Rodrigo Roa Duterte and Sara Z. Duterte.”
During his direct examination by private prosecutor James Bryan Alih, Galvez said the time deposit had a principal amount of P40,650,000.
Galvez said that the time deposit had 12 rollover periods or renewals. At the last renewal in February 2011, he said the amount already increased to P41.7 million, including the interest.

“If a time deposit certificate matures and is no longer renewed, the proceeds of the matured time deposit are credited to the settlement account,” Galvez said, affirming that the settlement account is the Julia Vargas Branch.
In March 2011, the BPI official said a credit and debit memo showed that a manager’s check was purchased for P41.7 million.
Galvez noted that a manager’s check has a period of validity of only six months.
Seven months after the purchase of the manager’s check, or in October 2011, Alih pointed out that another credit and debit memo reflected that a manager's check with the same amount was unutilized.

“When you say unutilized, Your Honor, ibig sabihin hindi po siya nagamit, depende sa sitwasyon. ‘Pag lumagpas ng six months nang hindi nagagamit ‘yung payee, kung kanino nakapangalan ang manager’s check, nasa desisyon ng payee kung nasa kanya na ang position ng manager’s check,” Galvez explained.

(When you say ‘unutilized,’ Your Honor, it means it wasn’t used, depending on the situation. If six months pass without the manager’s check being used, it is up to the payee or the person named on the check to decide what to do with it.)

“Puwede po ang kliyente, kung saan galing ang pondo na pinambili ng manager’s check, kung hindi na niya gagamitin ang manager’s check, puwede niyang i-request na ibalik po ito sa pinanggalingan ng account,” he added.
(The client, the one whose funds were used to purchase the manager’s check, can also request that the amount be returned to the source account if they no longer intend to use the check.)
Defense counsel Michael Poa objected to the presentation of evidence on the ground of relevance.
Alih said that the prosecution intends to prove a "pattern," that a transaction in 2011 moved around for several more years and was later on used to purchase insurance policies.

“We will attempt to show, Your Honor, that later, this amount—this P41 million, tapos meron pa pong (and an additional) P55 million, at some point, we will try to prove, magsasama sila ulit sa (they will be combined in the) Julia Vargas Branch, and they will use this to purchase several insurance policies for the same amount,” the private prosecutor said.

“Ang punto lang naman po eventually is that ‘yung manager’s check na pinapaikot, hindi nakikita sa year-end balance kasi naka-float ‘yung pera na ‘yun. ‘Yun lang naman ‘yung gusto naming i-establish as a baseline,” he added.
(The only point is that the manager's check that is being circulated is not reflected in the year-end balance because the money is already floating. That's all we want to establish as a baseline.)

To recall, former senator Antonio Trillanes IV claimed that the Vice President did not declare millions in time deposit assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) from 2007 to 2010 when she was Davao City vice mayor.
The former lawmaker said that, based on the research of his team, Sara Duterte had undeclared dollar and peso time deposits from 2007 until 2010.
He said the Vice President also did not declare a million dollars' worth of life insurance in her 2010 SALN.
Duterte's camp rejected the claims of Trillanes.
Duterte's spokesperson Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. said Trillanes has been repeatedly lying about the vice president and her family for years.

"Since 2016, former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV has been peddling the same exhausted lies regarding Extrajudicial Killings (EJKs), fabricated drug links, imaginary unexplained wealth, baseless corruption allegations, and fictional China connections against the Duterte family," Panelo said in a statement. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Teodoro, Nafarrete push for stronger military presence in Palawan
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. and Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) chief General Antonio Nafarrete called for a stronger and sustained military presence in Palawan during their visit to…

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 4:15pm

Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. and Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) chief General Antonio Nafarrete called for a stronger and sustained military presence in Palawan during their visit to the Western Command (WESCOM) in Puerto Princesa City.
Teodoro and Nafarrete visited WESCOM at Camp General Artemio Ricarte on Tuesday where they met with personnel and discussed the command’s operational requirements and defense posture.
“Palawan is the last frontier, right? Let’s make sure that it is the last frontier,” Teodoro said.
Teodoro said Palawan’s unique operating environment requires not only discipline and resolve but also creativity and innovation from military personnel.

For him, it is important to set up a significant tri-service presence in the area to support territorial defense, internal security operations, humanitarian assistance and disaster response, as well as deterrence against unlawful activities.
Teodoro said the government is working to strengthen the presence and capabilities of the Philippine Army and Philippine Marine Corps in Palawan.
This includes establishing at least a brigade-sized Army presence and developing a sustainable growth plan for the Marine Corps.
He said the Marine Corps needs mobility to maintain its firepower and operational effectiveness, particularly along the eastern seaboard where there is currently no significant military presence.

Meanwhile, Nafarrete also stressed the need for sustained military presence, operational readiness and strengthened capabilities in the country's western frontiers “to effectively safeguard the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.”

The AFP said the visit reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening WESCOM and supporting its personnel as they perform their mandate of protecting the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity. — RSJ, GMA News
